blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
There is a design flaw in all of us and nobody mentions it.

Your body cannot measure oxygen. It has no instrument for the one substance it cannot do without. What it measures instead is the waste — carbon dioxide, rising in the blood — and when that level crosses a line, a switch throws in the brainstem and the diaphragm begins firing on its own. That is the whole of the panic. That is the thing we call drowning, and terror, and the will to live.
It is an alarm wired to the exhaust rather than the tank, and it has never once had access to the fuel gauge.

I found that out while reading about freedivers and I have not been able to put it down since. Because of what follows from it: the terror is early. It arrives long before the danger. A trained person feels certain they are dying with most of their oxygen still in them, and if they do not answer the alarm, the alarm eventually stops — not because they have mastered anything, but because the brain has begun to run down and go quiet. And what people report from the other side of that switch is remarkably consistent, and remarkably calm, and nobody has ever satisfactorily explained it.
The standard explanation is that a brain low on fuel manufactures. That is almost certainly correct and it is not, on its own, an answer. It does not explain why the manufacturing agrees.

I wanted to write about people who go looking for that, and I wanted the going to be real. The training in this book is real training. The tables, the rock runs, the vests, the mechanics of a tow, the reason the foam will not hold a body, the sixty-eight seconds that is the worst survived hold-down in the sport’s recorded history — all of it is drawn from the documented accounts of people who have been there. The physiology is accurate. Where I have invented, I have tried to invent only in the places where the record genuinely goes quiet, which is further out than most people imagine.
The rest of the book is about what happens next, which is the part I could not stop thinking about.

If you find a state that reproduces — reliably, in every subject, on demand — you have not found a mystery. You have found a specification. And a specification can be built toward, and a thing that can be built toward can be made, and a thing that can be made can be sold. Everything that has ever been reached the hard way eventually becomes available the easy way, and I do not think that is a tragedy, and I am not certain it is not one either.
The body is the last honest witness we have. It is also, increasingly, a research site with a gift shop attached.

I am grateful to the big-wave community, whose courage I have borrowed and whose worst impulses I have exaggerated only slightly, and to the freedivers, who named the convulsion after a dance because there was nothing else to call it.
Chew Z
I. FLAT
ONE. BODY COUNT
The first thing you learn driving water patrol is that nobody you pull out is grateful.

They come up wrong. That’s the phrase, and it isn’t poetic, it’s diagnostic. A man who comes up right breaks the surface with his mouth already working, chin up, hands finding the sled before his eyes do. A man who comes up wrong arrives face-first with his arms behind him like something dropped from a truck, and his eyes are open, and there is nobody home behind them, and he is shaking. Not shivering. Shaking. A fine fast tremor through the shoulders and jaw, the whole body buzzing like a bad fluorescent tube.

They call that a samba. I didn’t know the word yet, that first winter. I just called it the shakes, which is what everyone on the beach called it, and everyone on the beach was wrong about most things.
I put the ski on its side and reached down and got a fistful of vest.

Kirill Novak, twenty-nine, Czech, sponsored by an energy drink whose logo was a stylized bolt of lightning going into a fist. He weighed a hundred and eighty pounds dry and about four hundred with the ocean in him. I hauled him across the sled and he vomited seawater onto my thigh and the shaking stopped, which is how you know it’s over, and then he said the thing they all say.
“I was fine.”
“You were fucking flatlining, Kirill.”
“I was fine. I had more.”

He had eleven seconds of more. I know because I count. That’s the job — not the pulling, any idiot with a throttle can pull. The job is the count. From the moment the lip lands on a man to the moment I put a hand on him, I run a number in my head, and that number is the only honest thing on this beach. Everything else is footage.
Kirill’s number was fifty-two. Fifty-two seconds.

Ask anyone in the parking lot how long a bad hold-down lasts and they’ll say two minutes, three minutes, they’ll tell you about a guy at Jaws who was down for four. It’s horseshit. It’s always horseshit.

Shane Dorian got the worst beating of his life at Mavericks in 2010, two waves on top of him, dragged across the reef at the end of a fifteen-foot leash, and when they timed the footage afterward he’d been under for one minute and eight seconds. Sixty-eight seconds. That’s the benchmark. That’s the story men tell in bars for the rest of their lives, and it’s shorter than a decent song intro.
So when a man tells you he had more, what he means is that he wanted more, and those are different animals entirely.

I’m forty-one. I drive a 2019 Yamaha with a sled bolted on the back and eleven hundred hours on the clock, most of them spent going nowhere at eight knots in water the colour of wet cement. I am not a surfer. I was, for about six years, in the way that a man who plays guitar in his kitchen is a musician. I had a sponsor once. They sent me stickers.

What I am is the guy with the hands. I can put a ski where a ski should not be able to go and take a man off the surface of the water at forty kilometres an hour without breaking his ribs, and I can do it in whitewater so aerated it barely qualifies as liquid — foam that won’t hold a hull, won’t hold a body, won’t hold anything, a slurry of air and salt that you don’t float in so much as fall through. That last part is the trick. Everyone can drive in green water. The channel is a car park. The zone is where the money is.
There are maybe forty people on earth who can do it well. I know eleven of them by name and I don’t like eight.

That day was a training day. Not a swell — a training day, which is what the crews call it when the buoys read twenty feet at fourteen seconds and the sponsors aren’t watching. Six-metre faces. Playground stuff, by the standards of the place. The kind of day where a man gets careless because nothing on the horizon is trying hard.

Kirill had been careless. He’d gone late on a set wave he had no business taking, got picked up by the lip and driven straight down onto the shelf, and the second wave of the set had landed on the exact patch of ocean where he was trying to become a person again.

He lay on the sled with his cheek on the pad and looked up at me with the specific expression I have come to know better than my own mother’s face. It is not fear. I want to be clear about that, because everyone gets this wrong, including the men themselves. It is not fear.
It’s the look of a man who has been interrupted.
“How long,” he said.
“Fifty-two.”
“That’s not—” He coughed. Salt water and something thicker. “That’s not right.”
“I count, Kirill.”
“That’s not right.” He wasn’t arguing. He was doing arithmetic, and losing.

I opened the throttle and took him in through the channel where the water goes flat and stupid, and behind us the ocean kept doing its thing without any of us, and up on the cliff about two hundred people in waterproof jackets took photographs of a man they thought had nearly died, when what had actually happened was much worse.
Here is what nobody tells you about drowning, and I mean the real mechanism, not the film version with the arms waving.
You don’t panic because you run out of air. You panic because of carbon dioxide.

That’s the whole thing. That’s the entire ugly secret of every human being who has ever been held under. Your body has no reliable way to measure oxygen. None. It’s a design flaw, and it’s in all of us, and there’s no patch coming. What your body measures instead is the waste — the carbon dioxide building up in your blood with nowhere to go. When that level climbs past a certain line, a switch throws in your brainstem and your diaphragm starts firing on its own, hard, in spasms, trying to make you breathe. It doesn’t ask. It’s not a suggestion.
Freedivers call that the struggle phase. Surfers call it “when it gets bad.”

And here’s the part that turns men into whatever Kirill was becoming: the struggle is a liar. Not about the danger — about the timing. When your diaphragm starts kicking, you typically still have a great deal of oxygen left. A trained man has minutes. An untrained man has more than he thinks. The convulsions arrive long before the lights go out.
Which means the terror is early. The terror is a false alarm that happens to be right often enough that we’ve kept it for four million years.
And that means the terror can be trained.

That’s not mysticism. That’s just tables — you hold your breath for a fixed time and shorten the rest between holds, again and again, until your blood is thick with the stuff and your body has to sit in that specific misery and learn that the misery is survivable. It’s the least glamorous training in sport. It’s lying on a yoga mat in a garage in your underwear, staring at a stopwatch, feeling like you’re being strangled by a friend.

Do it long enough and something moves. The alarm stops being an alarm. It becomes a doorway with a sign on it. And then one day, sooner or later, some part of you gets curious about what’s on the other side of the sign, and that is the day your life becomes a countdown that nobody else can see.
Kirill was somewhere around that day. So was everyone else in the crew, and I hadn’t worked it out yet, because I was busy counting.
I racked the ski at four. The gulls were doing their thing on the harbour wall, screaming at nothing, and the fish market smelled the way it always smells, which is like the inside of a wound.
Mina Sadr was sitting on the concrete steps with her hood up and her forearms on her knees, watching the water in a flat way, the way you’d watch a machine you’d been told to keep an eye on.
“Kirill?” she said.
“Fifty-two.”

She nodded slowly, and here’s the thing. She didn’t ask if he was okay. Nobody in that crew ever asked me if anyone was okay, not once, not one time in three years, and I had noticed and filed it under they’re assholes, because that was the simplest explanation and I was a simple man with a boat.
What she said was: “That’s good.”
Then she stood up and walked off toward the car park with her hands in her pockets, and I stood there smelling the fish market and holding a wet vest and understood exactly nothing.
TWO. THE POOL

The municipal pool in the old town opens to the public at six and closes at nine, and between nine and eleven on Tuesdays and Thursdays it belongs to a man named Renny Shaw, who pays for it in cash out of an envelope, and who has never in three years told anybody what the money is for.

It smells like every pool. Chlorine and armpit and something faintly sweet underneath, like a hospital that gave up. Twenty-five metres, six lanes, two metres deep at the far end, tiles the colour of an old swimming costume. There’s a mural of a dolphin on the wall that somebody painted in 1994 and nobody has had the courage to remove.

By nine-fifteen there were eight of them on the tiles and forty pounds of diving lead in a canvas bag by the blocks, and nobody was talking, which is the first thing you notice and the thing you never stop noticing. Eight athletes in a room and no noise. No music. No banter. In every other sport on earth a training room sounds like a bar at closing time. This sounded like a waiting area.

I was there because Renny paid me two hundred a session to sit on the lifeguard chair and count, and because Mina had asked me to, in the way she asked things, which was to state a fact and let you do the rest.
Tuesdays and Thursdays. Nine.
That was the whole invitation. That was, I understand now, the door being held open a crack, for a very long time, by someone who was hoping I’d have the decency to notice.
They started with tables. This is the unglamorous part and it takes forty minutes and if you filmed it you’d have nothing.
Two kinds. Everyone in that room knew the difference the way a carpenter knows a rip cut from a crosscut.

The first kind trains you to tolerate the poison. You hold your breath for a fixed time — say two minutes — and then you get a rest, and the rest gets shorter every round. Two minutes off. Then a minute forty-five. Then a minute thirty. Down and down until you’re going back under with your blood still dirty from the last one, still full of carbon dioxide you never got to blow off, and the misery starts at ten seconds instead of ninety. By the last round you’re not holding your breath so much as enduring an argument. That’s the point. You are teaching your body that the argument is survivable and does not require a verdict.

The second kind trains capacity. Fixed rest, growing hold. Two minutes, two-fifteen, two-thirty, up and up while your rest stays the same, so each round starts from clean blood and ends somewhere further out than the last. That one hurts less and terrifies more, because you can watch yourself go.
You do not do both on the same day. Anyone who tells you otherwise is either selling a course or trying to hurt you.
Renny ran the clock himself with a stopwatch that was older than half the people in the room, and he called the numbers in a voice with nothing in it at all.
“Ninety.”
“Sixty.”
“Thirty. Breathe up.”

Eight bodies on the tiles, face down at the edge, snorkels out, hands hanging in the gutter. When a person is deep into a table their fingers go a particular colour. Not blue. People say blue. It’s more of a grey-lilac, like the inside of a mussel shell, and it starts at the nail bed and creeps.
Around round six, the diaphragms started.

You can see it from a lifeguard chair better than you can see it from anywhere else on earth. The contraction goes through the whole torso — a single hard jolt at the base of the ribs, like someone’s punched them from inside. Then another, eight seconds later. Then closer together. By the last round it’s a rhythm, and the body on the tiles is jumping like a fish on a dock, and the face is perfectly still.
That’s the part I couldn’t get used to. The face. The body screaming and the face doing absolutely nothing.
Then the lead.

They call it rock running, and it’s about as sophisticated as the name. You take a breath, you get in, you sink to the bottom of the deep end holding forty pounds of dive weight, and you walk. Length of the pool, turn, walk back. The weight keeps you down. The walking raises your heart rate. A high heart rate burns oxygen the way an open throttle burns fuel, so you’re spending your one breath while doing exactly the thing that spends it fastest.
This is not a stunt. This is the closest a human being can get, in a municipal pool in a fishing town, to being held underwater by something that wants him dead.

Dorian said the thing that everyone quotes and almost nobody understands — that if you don’t know the science of holding your breath under pressure with a high heart rate, you go into a wipeout just hoping to survive, and that hoping is itself expensive. The hope raises your heart rate. The raised heart rate burns the oxygen. The fear is not a feeling. The fear is a fuel gauge, dropping.

So they walk. Up and down, in the grey-green light, past the drain covers, eight of them at staggered intervals so there’s always someone on the surface, a chain of grown adults trudging along the floor of a public swimming pool carrying weights like the world’s most depressing procession.

Beto Krall could do two lengths and part of a third. He was twenty-six and built like something drawn by a marketing department and he was the strongest man in the room by a distance and it did not help him at all, which nobody said out loud.
Mina Sadr did four.
She went in last, at ten past ten, when the others were sitting along the wall in towels with their heads back.
I want to describe this accurately because I’ve heard it described badly.

She breathed up for about two minutes and there was nothing dramatic about it — slow in through the nose, long out, longer each time, the exhale roughly twice the inhale. That’s all a breathe-up is. It isn’t loading up on oxygen; you can’t load up on oxygen, your blood is already almost full, that’s another thing everyone gets wrong. It’s about dropping your heart rate and getting your carbon dioxide down to a sensible floor so the alarm rings later. The dangerous version is when people overdo it — thirty fast breaths, hyperventilating — which blows off so much carbon dioxide that the alarm doesn’t ring at all. You feel wonderful. You feel like you could stay down forever. Then you black out without one second of warning and the ocean takes you while you’re still enjoying yourself.
Renny banned it. Renny banned it in the strongest language he ever used about anything, which was: we don’t do that.
Mina took her last breath and slid off the edge and sank, and picked up the bag, and started walking.

The first length was ordinary. The second length, the crew stopped talking, which I noticed because they hadn’t been talking. The third length her hands opened and closed twice on the handle and I saw the first contraction go through her, and I started my count over out of pure reflex.
Four lengths is a hundred metres. On the floor. Carrying lead.
She dropped the bag at the wall and did not come up.

She stood there. On the bottom of a swimming pool in the old town of a fishing village, in two metres of chlorinated water, with her arms loose at her sides and her chin slightly lifted, perfectly still, while her diaphragm fired hard enough that I could see it from twelve feet up.
Renny let the stopwatch run.

I said his name. He didn’t move. He was watching her the way you watch a pot you’re waiting on, and I will spend the rest of my life on the fact that he did not look worried, he looked interested, and there is no version of those two things that belong in the same man at the same moment.
At five minutes fifty on my count I came out of the chair.

She surfaced before I hit the water. Came up smooth, hands to the gutter, and did the recovery — sharp inhale, hold it, push down against a closed throat like you’re straining, which sounds insane but raises the pressure in your chest and shoves what oxygen you’ve got across into the blood before your brain finishes deciding whether to switch off. Hook breathing. Three of them, hard, then a fourth, and then her eyes came back on like a room being lit.
Nobody clapped. Nobody said anything.
She wiped her face and looked up at me still standing on the edge with my shoes on, and she smiled, which she almost never did, and she said:
“You always come out too early.”
And Renny Shaw wrote something in a black notebook.
THREE. RUY
My brother has been dead for nine years and I have never once described what he looked like when I brought him up, so I’m going to do it now and then I’m going to get on with the story.

He was twenty-six. He was better than me. That’s not modesty, that’s a ranking, and everyone who ever paddled out with the two of us could have told you inside a session. I had hands. Ruy had the other thing, the thing that can’t be trained and can’t be bought and mostly gets people killed — he had no negotiation in him. He looked at forty feet of moving water the way you’d look at a flight of stairs.
Our mother called him o teimoso. The stubborn one. She said it like a diagnosis.

It was the eleventh of February and the swell was not even the biggest of that winter. That’s the detail that people find hardest and I find easiest. It wasn’t the day. It was never going to be the day. It was a Tuesday with a long-period northwest swell and forty knots of nothing much, sixty-foot faces on the sets, and there were nine skis in the water and a hundred and forty people on the cliff, and a woman from a Portuguese television station was doing a piece to camera about tourism.

He went on the third wave of the set and got picked off at the top. Simple as that. Board went one way, he went the other, and the lip put him in the water somewhere I couldn’t see because there were fifteen feet of spray standing between me and the entire world.
I got to the foam at forty seconds.
I found him at fifty-eight.

He came up eight metres off my port side, face down, orange vest inflated — he’d fired the cord, which meant he’d been conscious enough to reach across his own chest and pull a toggle, which meant he was in there, which meant everything — and I had him on the sled by sixty-two.
Sixty-two seconds. Six seconds worse than Dorian’s, and Dorian walked up the beach and ate a sandwich.

Ruy was shaking when I got him. The buzz. The fine fast tremor. His eyes were open and he was looking at something over my shoulder that was not on my ski and not in the sky and not anywhere, and his mouth was moving, and I thought — and I want this on the record because I have thought about it every day for nine years — I thought he’s fine, he’s shaking, they always shake, the shaking means it’s ending.
I opened the throttle and took him in through the channel at sixty kilometres an hour because I wanted him on sand.
He talked the whole way. I couldn’t hear a word of it over the engine. His hand had my forearm and his grip was not weak, it was strong, it was the grip of a man making a point.

On the beach he stopped shaking, sat up on the wet sand in his vest with the water running off him, and looked at the ocean, and said — clearly, in Portuguese, in a perfectly normal voice, with two paramedics and a Sky Italia cameraman and his own brother listening —
“There’s a room down there.”
Then he said something else. Then he lay back on the sand and stopped.

Cardiac arrest. Twenty-six years old. The report said immersion pulmonary oedema secondary to breath-hold ascent and then a lot of other words, and the coroner explained to my mother in a small room with a plastic plant that sometimes the lungs fill from the inside, that the pressure changes do it, that it isn’t drowning in the way she was imagining, and my mother nodded politely the entire time because she was seventy and Portuguese and had been raised to be polite to men with clipboards.
They put on the death certificate that he drowned.
He didn’t drown. He drowned about as much as a man who falls off a roof dies of gravity.

I gave the interview. Of course I gave the interview. There is footage of me on a Portuguese news channel, thirty-two years old, wet, saying that my brother died doing what he loved, which is the single most repulsive sentence in the language and which I have never forgiven myself for, and the reporter asked me if I would be going back in the water.
I said I didn’t know.

I was back in the water in eleven weeks. Not surfing. Never surfing again, not once, not one wave since — driving. Patrol. Pulling other people’s brothers off the surface of the ocean at eleven hundred euros a weekend and counting the seconds out loud in my head like a man saying a rosary he doesn’t believe in.

The crews think that’s noble. There’s a version of me they’ve built where I’m the guy who lost someone and came back to make sure it doesn’t happen again, and I let them have it, because the alternative is to explain that I come back for the same reason a man who’s dropped his wedding ring down a drain keeps taking the U-bend apart. I am not out there to save anybody.
I’m out there because I want to know what the room is.
I never told anyone what he said. Not my mother, not the coroner, not one person in nine years of standing in car parks with these people.

Two paramedics heard it and thought it was the hypoxia talking, which it was, obviously, that’s what oxygen starvation does — the brain in the dark starts building. It hallucinates. Every freediver knows it, every high-altitude climber knows it, every man who has ever been held under too long comes up with a story about light or a corridor or a voice, and the medical explanation is a shrug: a brain running out of fuel will manufacture, because a brain cannot do nothing.
That’s the sane reading. I’ve held onto it the way you hold a handrail.
But the second thing he said, the thing after the room, was six words, and neither of the paramedics spoke Portuguese well enough to catch them, and the cameraman was rewinding.
I caught them.
I’ll get to them.
FOUR. DELIVERABLES

Beto Krall’s sponsor meeting was held in a function room above a restaurant that does grilled sardines for tourists, and I was there because Beto asked me to drive him and because I am weak about free food.

Three of them flew in. A brand manager called Antonia, a man from the agency whose job title was Head of Athlete Narrative, and a girl in her twenties with a laptop who never said one word for ninety minutes and typed continuously, which was somehow the most frightening thing in the room.
They had a deck. Of course they had a deck.

Slide four was a photograph of Beto being obliterated. It was a good photograph. Nazaré, two winters ago, forty-foot face, Beto at the bottom of it in the exact posture of a man being deleted, the whitewater already over his head, the board vertical in the air behind him like a headstone that hadn’t landed yet.
“This,” said the Head of Athlete Narrative, “is our best-performing asset of all time.”
Beto nodded. He was twenty-six and he had a jaw you could open letters with and he genuinely did not understand what he’d just been told.
“Four point one million organic,” Antonia said. “For comparison, his win at Punta Galea did seven hundred K.”
So there it is. That’s the industry, stated out loud in a room with a whiteboard, and nobody flinched, and the sardines came up on a plate with lemon.
The rides do seven hundred thousand. The beatings do four million.

Which means every man on that beach is being paid — not officially, not in a contract you could take to a lawyer, but paid nonetheless, in the only currency that has ever mattered to a sponsored athlete, which is renewal — to fail spectacularly on camera at regular intervals.

They don’t put it like that. What they put in the contract is a number of what they call content-eligible sessions and a number of hero moments, and if you asked Antonia to define a hero moment she would say something about authenticity and emotional truth, and if you looked at the last four years of what actually got posted you would find that a hero moment is a man disappearing under a mountain of water and the crowd on the cliff going oohhh in eleven languages.
I ate my sardines.
There’s a thing I’ve watched happen to about a dozen young men and two young women in this town and I’ve never seen it go the other way.

Year one, the kid is terrified and honest about it. He’ll tell you at the bar, three beers in, that he nearly shat himself on the second wave and that he doesn’t know if he’s built for this. This is the healthiest he will ever be.
Year two, he stops saying that. He’s learned the vocabulary. He says things like I felt really connected out there today.

Year three, he starts describing the beatings as the good part. And here’s what’s diabolical about it, here is the actual machinery: he isn’t lying. By year three he has taken so many that his body has quietly recalibrated, the way a man who works in a slaughterhouse stops smelling the slaughterhouse, and the hold-downs that used to run him through with terror now arrive with something else attached. Something with a flavour. And when the sponsor’s money and the crowd’s noise and his own nervous system all start pointing in the same direction at once, the kid does not stand a chance, because there is nothing in his life telling him to stop except a forty-one-year-old ski driver with a chip on his shoulder who he thinks is a bit of a cunt.
Year four is where they either quit, or they find Renny.
“They want twelve,” Beto said in the car park afterwards.
“Twelve what?”
“Content-eligible. Season.” He was rolling a cigarette on the seat of the truck, which he did badly, because he was an athlete and rolling cigarettes is a skill of the unfit. “And two hero.”
“Two.”
“Minimum two.” He licked the paper. “Bro, it’s fine. That’s like — that’s nothing. I’ll get two in a fortnight if the Farol lights up.”
“Beto.” I waited until he looked at me. “You understand what you just agreed to.”

“Yeah, I do.” Total ease. No defence in it, none, and that’s what made it awful, because a defensive man can still be argued with. “I agreed to eat shit twice on camera for a hundred and forty grand and a truck. Cass, what do you think the alternative is? Fishing?”
He lit the cigarette. It went out. He lit it again.
“Anyway,” he said, “it’s not even the worst part of my week.”
“What’s the worst part of your week?”

And Beto Krall, twenty-six, four point one million organic, looked out through the windscreen at the fish market and said, “Tuesdays,” and laughed, and did not explain, and I did not ask, because I was a simple man with a boat and I thought I already knew what Tuesdays were.
Tuesdays were a swimming pool with a dolphin painted on the wall.
PROTOCOL I. TABLES
Read this once and then do not read it again. Reading is not the work.
PURPOSE. To render the alarm inert.

The alarm is carbon dioxide. It is not drowning, it is not death, it is not the ocean. It is a chemical rising in the blood and a switch in the brainstem that has not been redesigned in four million years. You have been obeying an unmaintained system your entire life. We are going to stop.

Understand what you actually have. A trained adult at rest, on one breath, holds enough oxygen for between four and six minutes of consciousness. In cold water, with the face immersed, more — the heart slows, blood withdraws from the limbs to the core, the spleen contracts and releases stored red cells into circulation. Your body has an emergency reserve it does not tell you about. The alarm rings anyway. The alarm has never once had access to the fuel gauge.

TABLE ONE — TOLERANCE. Eight rounds. Hold fixed at your comfortable maximum minus thirty seconds. Rest begins at two minutes and reduces by fifteen seconds each round. Round eight will be unpleasant at ten seconds. This is correct. You are not being harmed. You are being informed.

TABLE TWO — CAPACITY. Eight rounds. Rest fixed at two minutes. Hold increases by fifteen seconds each round. Table Two is for Sunday. Never the same day as Table One. A man who runs both in one day is not training, he is auditioning for something.

CONTRAINDICATED ABSOLUTELY. Hyperventilation. Fast breathing before a hold. It feels magnificent. It removes the carbon dioxide without adding one millilitre of oxygen, which means it removes the alarm and not the danger. You will feel calm and capable straight through the floor and into unconsciousness with no warning whatsoever. Men die this way in swimming pools, in three feet of water, in front of their children. We do not do that. Anyone found doing it is finished here.

RECOVERY. On surfacing: sharp inhale, close the throat, press down against it for two seconds, release. Repeat three times. This raises the pressure inside the chest and drives oxygen across into the blood before the brain completes its decision to shut down. The three seconds after surfacing kill more divers than the three minutes underneath.
PROGRESS. Do not measure yourself against the athletes. Measure yourself against the record, which is the only honest ceiling.

On air, motionless, no oxygen assistance: Stéphane Mifsud, eleven minutes thirty-five seconds, Hyères, 2009. Lung capacity measured at ten and a half litres. Branko Petrović, eleven fifty-four, Dubai, 2014.

You will read about longer numbers. Twenty-four minutes. Twenty-nine minutes. Ignore them. Those men breathed pure oxygen for half an hour first, which floods the lungs with roughly six times the usable fuel and turns the whole event into an exercise in stillness rather than an exercise in tolerance. It is a different sport. It is a magic trick with a supply line.
We are interested in what a man contains, not what he is issued.

A NOTE ON DISCOMFORT. Around round six of Table One the diaphragm will begin to contract on its own. It will feel like being punched from the inside at decreasing intervals. Trainees describe it as panic. It is not panic. Panic is a decision you make about a sensation.
The contractions are a door knocking.
You are not required to answer it.
Not yet.
— R.S.
FIVE. DRY
Renny Shaw does not go in the water.

Not won’t — doesn’t. There’s a difference and he made me understand it one evening in November in the back room of a bar called the Baleia, where he drank tea and I drank beer and the rain came sideways off the Atlantic and hit the window like handfuls of gravel.

He was fifty-eight. Tall, narrow, grey stubble kept at the exact same length for three years, which means he cut it every second day and never let it be anything. Hands like a man who’d done work. He wore the same fleece constantly and I never once smelled anything on him, not sweat, not soap, nothing, which I noticed because everyone in a fishing town smells of something.
Twenty-two years as a diving medical technician for the navy. That’s the actual job title. He described it once, flatly, as the man who sits in the chamber with you while they take the pressure off.
“You’ve never surfed,” I said.
“I surfed until I was thirty-one.”
“And?”
“And I stopped.” He turned the cup around on the saucer. “I got very interested in a different part of it.”
“Which part.”
“The part underneath.”
Rain on the window. Somebody in the front bar losing at cards, loudly.

“There is a lot of literature,” Renny said, “on what a human being is doing during the two minutes before he dies of asphyxia. There is almost none on what he is experiencing. Do you understand the distinction? We have measured every parameter of that body. Partial pressures, cardiac output, cerebral perfusion, the lot. We know precisely what is happening to the machine.” He looked up. “Nobody has ever written down what the man saw. Because the ones who could tell you are, as a class, dead, and the ones who come back have been given a very effective explanation for why what they saw doesn’t count.”
“Which is what?”

“Hypoxia.” He said the word the way you’d hand somebody a coat. “Oxygen starvation. The brain, deprived, generates imagery. It is a complete explanation, Cass. It explains everything, it predicts nothing, and it has closed the file on roughly four thousand years of testimony.”
I said that I’d been under, and it wasn’t a room, it was just black and horrible.
“How long?”
“Thirty, forty seconds. Long enough.”

“No.” He smiled for the first time, and it was not warm, it was the smile of a man being handed exactly the sentence he’d been waiting for. “That’s not long enough. That’s nothing. That’s the vestibule. You have never been anywhere.”
He didn’t ride, and here’s the reason, and it took me two more years to understand that he gave it to me straight that night and I filed it wrong.

“I can’t,” he said. “I’ve been decompressed eleven times. Both eardrums are patched. My left lung has scarring across the lower lobe from an incident in 1997 that I’m not going to describe to you over a beer.” He tapped his sternum twice with two fingers, a clinician’s gesture, a percussion on his own chest. “The machine’s had it. I’d get to ninety seconds and I’d be finished.”
“So you send other people.”
“I train other people.” He didn’t blink. “You’d like there to be a difference and I’d like there to be a difference. I’ve decided to be careful about what I claim.”

That was, I realise now, the most honest thing anybody said to me in three years. He told me exactly what he was. He did it with tea in front of him and rain on the glass and no defensiveness whatsoever, and I heard it as humility.
He talked about the athletes like a foreman talking about a fleet.

Kirill: good engine, no instrument panel. Meaning tolerance without self-knowledge, meaning a man who could suffer indefinitely and had no idea what any of the suffering meant, which made him useless for what Renny actually wanted and perfect for what Renny publicly claimed to want.

Beto: strength is a liability here. Big muscles burn oxygen. The best static breath-hold athletes are not built like Beto Krall, they are built like accountants — Renny’s word — long-lunged, low-mass, unremarkable men who can lie still. Muscle is a fuel cost. Beto’s entire body was working against him and his sponsors were paying him for the body.
Mina: he didn’t say anything about Mina. I asked directly, twice. First time he changed the subject. Second time he said, “Mina’s not an athlete,” and went to the bar.
Walking out, I asked him what he’d written in the notebook the night she did the four lengths.
“Her time.”
“You were writing for a while for a time.”
“Her time,” he said, “and what she said afterwards.”
“She said I come out too early.”
“Yes.” He put his hand on the door. “You do.”

He held it open for me, which was courteous, and I walked out into the rain thinking he’d made a joke about my driving, and it was six weeks before I understood that he had just told me, plainly and without cruelty, that I had been killing people since 2016.
SIX. THE WORD

The first time I heard it said properly was a Thursday in the pool, and it came out of Renny in the middle of a sentence about something else, the way a word does when it belongs to you and you’ve forgotten other people don’t have it.

A kid called Dario had come up bad off a rock run. Grey-lilac fingers, arms not working, that fine fast buzz through the jaw. Two of them had him under the armpits at the gutter and Renny was standing over the tiles with the stopwatch still going and he said:
“He’s sambaing. Don’t lift him. Keep the airway clear and let it finish.”
And I said, from the chair, like an idiot: “He’s what?”
Renny didn’t look up.

“Samba,” he said. “Hypoxic convulsion. The brain’s low enough on oxygen that motor control goes, but not so low that consciousness has gone — not quite yet. The body shakes. Freedivers named it after the dance.” He crouched, turned the kid’s head slightly with one hand. “It’s the last warning you get. If it goes on, he’ll black out. If we handle it properly he’ll be talking to us in twenty seconds and he’ll remember none of this.”
Dario shook on the wet tiles for another eleven seconds, then stopped, then said something in Italian, then asked what time it was.
Renny wrote in the notebook.
I sat back in the chair and something reorganised itself in my chest, quietly, the way a building settles.
Here’s why.
Surfing has no word for that.

I want to be precise. Surfing has fifty words for the beating. We say rag-dolled, which is a body going limp and thrown around. We say Maytagged, after the washing machine. We say worked, drilled, pounded, cleaned up, caught inside. We have a whole comic vocabulary for it and every single term is a joke, because for eighty years the culture’s entire relationship with nearly dying was to make it small at the bar afterwards. You got worked. Have a beer.

Freediving has a name for the convulsion. A clinical name, with a mechanism attached, and a protocol, and a decision tree. Because freedivers aren’t surviving the thing, they’re studying it. They’ve been down there with clipboards.

So when a man in a swimming pool in a Portuguese fishing town stands over a twitching twenty-two-year-old and says he’s sambaing, don’t lift him, let it finish, what he is telling you — if you have ears — is that these people have stopped being surfers.
Surfers get worked and go in for a beer.
These people had a taxonomy.
You do not build a taxonomy for something you are trying to avoid. You build a taxonomy for something you intend to visit repeatedly and want to be able to discuss precisely afterwards.
That was the Thursday. That was the moment, and I did nothing about it for eight months, and Beto Krall died.

I did ask, though. Give me that much. On the way out to the car park with the chlorine coming off my clothes I asked Renny whether the pool work was actually making anyone safer in the water, because I’d been pulling the same men out of the same foam for three years and the numbers hadn’t moved.
He seemed pleased I’d asked.
“That’s a good question and the answer’s no.”
“No?”

“The correlation is very poor. A man with a six-minute static in a warm pool may fail at forty seconds in the impact zone, because the pool has no cold, no current, no board, no leash, no rock, no adrenaline and no belief that he’s about to die. All of which cost oxygen.” He was unlocking his van. “The training is not the thing, Cass. The training is the price of admission for the thing.”
“Then what’s the thing?”
Renny Shaw thought about it for slightly too long. In the sodium light his face was the colour of a fish.
“Familiarity,” he said.
And drove off.
Familiarity. I turned that word over the whole way home and got nothing out of it, because I assumed he meant familiarity with fear.
He didn’t. He meant it the way you’d mean it about a place.
SEVEN. MINA’S ROOM
Mina Sadr rented the top floor of a house on the Rua da Cerca from a widow who kept pigeons, and I went up there exactly twice, and the second time is the one that matters.

She was thirty. Born in Karaj, raised in Gothenburg, in Portugal seven years on a residency card she’d got through a work arrangement that I never fully understood and which I suspect was mostly a lie told very carefully to a bored official. She had been, in order: a competitive swimmer until fifteen, a person who did not leave a bedroom for most of a year at nineteen, a dive instructor in Dahab, a spearfisher, and then this.
She was the deepest on the Protocol and everyone knew it including the men, who dealt with it the way men deal with such things, which is by not mentioning it in a specific and effortful way.

The flat had two chairs, a mattress, a hot plate, a wall of hooks with wetsuits on them, and a smell of neoprene that got into your sinuses and stayed for a day. On the windowsill: a laptop, a stopwatch, and a plastic pulse oximeter, the kind you clip on a fingertip, that reads the oxygen saturation in your blood as a percentage.
Ninety-eight is normal. Ninety-five, a doctor takes an interest. Below ninety, a hospital gets involved.
Hers was set to log. There was a cable.
“You want tea,” she said. It wasn’t a question, it was an announcement of what was going to happen.
I said I’d come to talk about Kirill, which was true and also not the reason.
“Kirill’s going to be dead in two years,” she said, filling the pan. “He’ll do it in Chile. He wants a big audience but he’s too proud to go where the good drivers are.”
“Jesus Christ, Mina.”
“You asked.”
“I hadn’t asked yet.”
“You’d asked.” She put the pan on the hot plate. “Everyone asks with their face first. It’s very tiring.”

That was her. Flat, exact, no cruelty in it and no cushioning either. I’ve thought a lot about why she was the only person in that whole circus I could stand and I think it’s because she never once performed the beach. Never said stoked, never said energy, never described the ocean as a woman or a mother or a teacher. She talked about it like weather and machinery, and about her own body like a rented vehicle she was returning at some point with the mileage noted.
The notebook was on the second chair.
Not Renny’s — a copy. Or a sibling. Same black cover, same cheap elastic, and I’d watched Renny write in one of those roughly four hundred times.
She saw me see it. She did not move it.
“You can look,” she said. “You won’t understand it.”
I picked it up.
Columns. Ruled by hand with a straight edge, page after page, going back years.
DATE. SUBJECT. VEHICLE. T-DOWN. T-REC. Δ. NOTES.

The dates ran to nearly a decade. The subjects were initials. VEHICLE was a column I couldn’t parse at all — sometimes POOL, sometimes N/PN, sometimes MAV, sometimes just TOW. T-DOWN and T-REC were times in seconds, and the Δ between them was done in a different pen, later, in a smaller hand.
The NOTES column was mostly blank. When it wasn’t blank, it was short.
corridor, warm, not frightened stairs. counted them. the room. angle from below. same as KN 3/2. verify. nothing. wasted.
I stood in a rented flat that smelled of neoprene holding somebody’s homework and felt the floor go a little soft.
Because the room was in there. In a stranger’s handwriting. Twice on the page I was looking at and I hadn’t turned back yet.
“What is this.”
“It’s the ledger.”
“Mina, what is this.”
She took the pan off the heat. She didn’t turn around.
“It’s what happens,” she said, “when you stop assuming the hypoxia is noise and start assuming it’s signal. That’s all it is. It’s the least mystical thing in this town. It’s a spreadsheet.”
“You’re writing down hallucinations.”

“We’re writing down reports.” She poured. “If four people who have never met describe the same feature, in the same orientation, at the same depth of oxygen debt, then at minimum you’ve found something reproducible about human brains. At minimum. That’s a neurology paper, Cass, that’s not a religion.” She handed me a glass. “It’s only a religion if you decide what it means. We haven’t decided.”
“What does Renny think it means?”
She sat down on the mattress with her back against the wall.

“Renny thinks,” she said, “that we have all been standing outside a building for four million years, and that the alarm is on the door, and that everyone who has ever got past the alarm was too frightened at the time to look at the architecture.”
“And you?”
“I think it’s a spreadsheet.”

She drank her tea. She looked at me over the top of the glass with those flat grey eyes and I have gone over this moment more times than any other in my life and I am still not certain whether she was lying to me or to herself, and I have come to think that at that point in the winter she genuinely did not know either.
At the door I asked the question I’d come to ask, which had been sitting in my mouth since the pool.
“Whose handwriting is at the front? The early stuff. Before the dates go into the pool sessions.”
Mina Sadr stood in the doorway with the pigeons going off downstairs.
“You should ask Renny that,” she said.
And shut the door with real gentleness, which is how I knew.
EIGHT. BUOY 62081

On the ninth of December at four in the morning a weather buoy anchored in four thousand metres of water west of Ireland reported a significant wave height of fourteen point six metres at a period of twenty-two seconds, and every phone in the town went off inside ninety minutes.
I want to explain what those numbers mean, because they are the two most important numbers in this book and everybody outside the sport gets them backwards.

Significant wave height is not the height of the biggest wave. It’s roughly the average of the biggest third. So fourteen point six metres offshore means the sea out there is running at an average of forty-eight feet in the top third, and the outliers in that field will be half again as large, and none of it has broken yet — it’s just swell, moving.

Period is the gap in seconds between one crest and the next, and it is everything. It tells you how deep the energy runs. A short-period swell, eight or ten seconds, is wind chop: it lives near the surface and dies on the first shallow thing it meets. A twenty-two-second swell is a wall of moving water extending hundreds of metres down. It doesn’t feel the seabed until the seabed is genuinely serious. It crosses an ocean and loses almost nothing.
Twenty-two seconds is very rare. Twenty-two seconds with fourteen metres behind it is a phone call at four in the morning.
And here is the local part.

There is a canyon offshore of this town. Two hundred and thirty kilometres long, the largest in Europe, and it ends — not near, ends — directly beneath the beach under the lighthouse. Five thousand metres of trench running straight at the sand like a rifle barrel.

Swell crossing that canyon stays in deep water the whole way in. It arrives at full strength, undissipated, with none of the gradual grinding-down that a normal continental shelf performs over fifty kilometres. Meanwhile the same swell to the side of the canyon has been over shallow ground, has slowed, has bent. The two trains meet at the head of the canyon at slightly different speeds and slightly different angles and they stack — one wave climbing onto the back of another, adding heights that were never supposed to be added. On top of that the beach throws a hard backwash seaward off the cliff, and the incoming wave hits that outgoing water and jacks vertical, all at once, with no warning ramp.
That’s it. That’s the entire magic trick. There’s no mysticism in it. It’s a funnel, a collision and a ricochet.

It is why a Hawaiian rode a seventy-eight-foot wave here in 2011 and Guinness put it in a book. It’s why a Brazilian got eighty out of it six years later, and a German got eighty-six in 2020, and why in the spring of 2024 somebody measured a face at ninety-three feet and change and the ratification committee argued about it for a year. It’s why an eighteen-year-old Portuguese kid rode something in October 2020 that a university team afterwards put at over a hundred feet, which was never certified, which nobody will ever settle.
That last one matters to this story. Hold onto it.
The biggest thing that has ever happened here is a thing that cannot be measured, and everyone involved has learned to live with that.
Two days out.

The models had been showing the bruise for a week before the buoy confirmed it, which is what a twenty-two-second period buys you: warning. They disagreed for the first two days — the American one wanted it further north, the European one had it landing on us square — and then on day three they converged, and after that it was just arithmetic and dread.
The town changes in those eight days and it’s not subtle.

Hotel prices triple. The two mechanics stop answering the phone. Vans arrive from Biarritz and Ericeira and Newquay with boards on the roof that cost more than the vans. The bar fills with men in technical outerwear standing in circles saying numbers to each other — twenty-two at one-ninety, high tide’s at eleven-forty, there’s a secondary at fourteen — the way old men in other towns discuss horses.
And the crews go quiet.

That’s the tell. In week one of a normal swell everyone’s loud. In week one of a big one they get polite. People start settling small debts. Beto Krall paid me a hundred and ten euros he’d owed me since August, in cash, unasked, and made a joke about it, and the joke wasn’t good.

I did my checks on the tenth. New impellor, spare plugs, sled straps, radio, two knives, one on the ski and one on my calf, because the only thing worse than a man in the foam is a man in the foam attached to five metres of leash and a buoyant board that wants to be somewhere else.
Renny came down the slipway carrying two fuel cans and set them on the concrete and stood looking at the water with his hands in his fleece.
The horizon was doing that thing it does before. Nothing yet. Just a slightly wrong texture out past the point, like a page held at an angle.
“They’ll all be down there this week,” he said.
I thought he meant in the impact zone.
“Some of them for a long time,” he said.
I thought he meant hold-downs.
I went and got the second fuel can, and behind me Renny Shaw, who had never once in three years asked me a personal question, said:
“Cass. Your brother. When you brought him in.”
I stopped walking.
“How long was he under?”
“Sixty-two seconds.”
“And when you reached him, was he moving?”
The gulls. The slipway. The wrong-textured horizon.
“He’d fired his vest,” I said.
“That isn’t what I asked.”

I didn’t answer him. I picked up the fuel can and carried it to the ski and did not look at him for the rest of the afternoon, and that night I lay awake in a flat above a garage with the window open, listening for the sound the ocean makes about a day before it arrives — a low knock in the harbour wall, spaced out, patient, like something checking whether anyone’s home.
END OF PART ONE
II. SWELL
NINE. NAPAT
Two days out, the slipway looks like a war that hasn’t been declared.

Nine skis on trailers. Fuel drums. A man from Peniche selling impellers out of the back of a Transit at eighty euros over retail because he can. Boards laid on foam blocks in rows — and they don’t look like surfboards, that’s the thing nobody expects. A tow board is six feet long, narrow as a plank, weighted with lead in the nose, and it has footstraps. It weighs what a child weighs. You could not paddle it across a swimming pool. It exists to be dragged to speed by an engine and then to hold a line on a face steep enough to be called a cliff in any other context.
The vests come out of the cars last, and everybody handles them the same way, which is carefully, and nobody makes eye contact while they’re doing it.
Here’s the vest, because it matters later.

It’s a neoprene shell worn under the wetsuit top with two bladders in it, one across the chest and one at the upper back, and a small steel cartridge of compressed carbon dioxide in a housing at the ribs. There’s a toggle on a short cord at the left hip. You pull it, a pin punctures the cartridge, and the bladders inflate in under a second and haul you toward the surface at a speed you don’t control. Riders call it pulling the cord.

Shane Dorian designed the first one after Mavericks in 2010 put two waves on him and dragged him across the reef for sixty-eight seconds. He came up nauseous and concussed and inside a year he’d built the thing.
It saves lives. It has saved lives all along this coast, including three I know by name.

And it’s why everything after 2011 got worse. Because the moment you hand a man a device that will take him up, you have also handed him permission to go somewhere he otherwise wouldn’t. That’s not a criticism of Dorian, who is a serious person and was solving a real problem. It’s just what happens to every safety invention in every sport that has ever existed. The equipment doesn’t reduce the risk. It relocates it further out, and then everybody follows it.
There’s one cartridge in the vest. One. You get a single pull.
There is a term for a man who has used his cartridge and is still in the impact zone with a set coming, and the term is a passenger.
Renny’s ski sat at the top of the slip, and I’d looked at it two hundred times without reading it.
An older Yamaha, immaculate, no sponsor decals, engine cover matte black. Along the port sponson, in small hand-painted letters, white on black, in a font that was nobody’s brand:
NAPAT
I asked him what it meant.
“It’s a name.”
“Whose?”
Renny was checking a strap. He didn’t look up and he didn’t pause, and he said it the way a man reads a bus timetable.

“There’s an old Persian figure. Apam Napat. It means Child of the Waters. He lives at the bottom of the sea and he holds a thing called the khvarenah — the glory. It’s a kind of light that belongs to kings and to the world, and at some point in the story it runs away from a man who doesn’t deserve it, and it goes into the water, and it stays there.”
“And?”
“And men dive for it.” He pulled the strap tight. “Three brothers, in one version. They go down for it in turn.”
“Do they get it?”
“No.”
He rolled the trailer forward six inches and set the chock.
“Nobody gets it,” he said. “That’s the point of the story. It’s down there, it’s real, it’s the actual glory of the world, and it will not be taken by anybody who goes down after it.”
I said that seemed like a shit name for a rescue ski.
“It’s a very good name for a rescue ski,” Renny said, and went to get coffee.
I did my own kit that afternoon.

Two knives. One taped inverted to the handlebar mount where I can reach it with either hand, one in a sheath on my right calf. Both serrated, both cheap, both replaced every season because saltwater eats everything and a knife you trust is a knife you’ve replaced.
The knives are for leashes.

Nobody outside the sport understands this and it upsets people when you explain it, so I mostly don’t. A rider goes down attached to five metres of urethane cord and a buoyant board. In broken water the board becomes a sea anchor with a mind of its own — it gets caught in the outflow and it pulls, and the man on the other end of it goes wherever it decides, usually down, usually across the shelf. Dorian’s worst moment happened at the end of a fifteen-foot leash. Half the tow riders here won’t wear one at all for exactly this reason and the other half won’t go without.
So: when I get to a man, before anything else, I cut. Board goes. Board can be replaced by a phone call. Then I get a hand into the vest and put him on the sled.
Cut, grip, throttle. Three moves. I can do them in four seconds in flat water and I have done them in eleven in conditions where I could not see my own front hatch.

Radio check. Spare plugs in a dry bag taped inside the hull. Tow rope coiled and stowed, never loose, because a loose rope in the foam finds the intake, and a ski with a rope in its intake is a very expensive raft with two people clinging to it.
Fuel: full, twice, because a ski in the zone burns fuel at a rate that would embarrass a helicopter, and because the day you run dry is the day you find out what the count really means.
Mina came down at six with a bag over her shoulder and sat on the wall.
She watched me tape the second knife.
“How many did you pull last winter?”
“Thirty-one.”
“How many were dead?”
“None.”
“How many should have been?”
I put the tape down.
“Four,” I said.
She nodded, like a woman ticking a box.
“And how many of the four came up talking?”

I looked at her for a long moment. Out past the point the horizon had that texture again, wrong, like a page held at an angle, and the knock had started in the harbour wall, and it was spaced further apart than yesterday, which meant the period was lengthening, which meant it was coming.
“Three,” I said.
Mina Sadr picked up her bag.
“Renny has all three,” she said. “You should ask to see what they said.”
TEN. FIRST DAY
It arrived overnight on the eleventh, the way it always does, so that the first you know of it is the sound.

I woke at five to a noise like a goods train being unloaded somewhere under the floor. Not a crash. Nothing so tidy. A long low tearing, four or five seconds of it, then quiet, then another. You feel it in the window glass before you hear it. Everyone in this town sleeps through storms and nobody sleeps through that.

Fifty-five, sixty-foot faces on the sets by first light. Not the big day. Everyone said so, all morning, in the specific tone of men reassuring themselves — this isn’t even it, this is the front edge, Thursday’s the one. The lighthouse had two hundred people on it at seven-fifteen in the dark and the rain.
I want to try to give you the scale honestly, because photographs lie about this in both directions.

A sixty-foot face is a six-storey building that is moving at forty kilometres an hour and is made of something that weighs a ton per cubic metre. The lip — the part that throws forward off the top — comes over in a slab. On a normal wave the lip is a curl. On this thing it’s a section of roof. When it lands it does not splash; it detonates, and the sound arrives at the cliff two full seconds later, and the whole headland transmits it up through your boots.

Between the sets the water in the impact zone isn’t water. That’s the part nobody photographs because it doesn’t photograph. It’s aerated foam — a suspension of air in seawater, sometimes forty percent gas by volume, the colour of dirty milk and the consistency of nothing at all. A body doesn’t float in it. A hull doesn’t plane on it. A vest with two litres of gas in it will lift a man through green water like a cork and will lift him through that stuff slowly, if at all, because there’s nothing there to push against.

That’s the actual killer. Not the wave. The wave passes in eleven seconds. The foam is where men die, and it can be a hundred metres wide, and while you are in it you are inside a fluid that has stopped agreeing to be a fluid.
The tow is a two-person thing and it’s more like aerial refuelling than like surfing.

Rider in the water on the board with his feet in the straps, holding a handle on a rope about thirty metres long. Driver runs the ski up-swell to build speed, then swings a wide arc and puts the rider onto the face of a wave that is still gathering, still hasn’t decided to break, at a point about a third of the way down its length. You need forty, fifty kilometres an hour of board speed — you cannot paddle into these, no human arm generates enough velocity to match a wave moving that fast, which is the entire reason the sport exists in this form.
Then the whip.

The driver banks hard off the face at the last moment, which slingshots the rider forward and across, and the rider lets go of the handle at the exact instant the wave takes him. Too early and he sinks off the back. Too late and the rope pulls him off his line into the pit.

After that the driver has about four seconds to get himself out of a place he should not be, up and over the shoulder of a wave that is about to fall over, and into the channel — the deep water off to the side where the canyon runs and things stay comparatively sane.
Then the driver turns around and watches his friend.
That’s the job. You put him in, you get out, and then you sit in the channel at idle and watch, and if it goes wrong you go into the worst water on earth on purpose while the next one is coming.
Beto went at eight-forty on a set wave that stood up out of nothing.
I want to describe this properly because of what happened four days later.

The wave came in off the canyon and jacked — that instant vertical rise when incoming water hits the backwash coming off the beach. There’s no ramp to it. One second it’s a hill and the next it’s a wall with an overhang, and Beto was already on it, in the top third, with his knees soft and his left hand out behind him.

Sixty feet under his feet. A man the size of a pencil mark. Behind him the lip started to throw and the whole top of the wave came out over him like a shelf being pushed off a building, and he outran it — down the face at a shallow angle, faster than anything on water has a right to go, spray coming off his rail in a plume that the wind took forty metres sideways.
He made it. Straight out the front into the flat, kicked off, arms up.
The cliff went off. Two hundred people making a noise you could hear over a sixty-foot wave.

I picked him up in the channel and he was laughing, absolutely lit, gripping my shoulder with a hand like a clamp, saying did you see it, did you fucking see it, and I said I saw it, and I meant it, and for about ninety seconds on the eleventh of December I was as happy as anyone in that town.

Because that’s the other half. I don’t want to be dishonest about this book. If it were all ledgers and swimming pools nobody would come. What Beto Krall did that morning was one of the most beautiful things a human being can do and it took eleven seconds and it will outlive him and everyone who saw it.
Kirill went down at eleven and I got him at thirty-eight seconds. Fine. Ordinary. He swore at me.
A Basque kid called Iker went down at half past twelve and I got him at nineteen, and he was so relaxed about it he asked me to take him back out rather than in.
And at two-ten, in a lull, with the sets fifteen minutes apart and the sun trying, Mina Sadr paddled out.
Paddled. On a gun — a proper big-wave paddle board, ten foot two, which she had carried down the beach herself.
Nobody tows on a lull. There’s nothing to tow into. What she was doing was sitting in the impact zone, alone, on a board, in a lull, waiting for a set she had no realistic chance of catching.
I ran the ski over and idled twenty metres off.
“What are you doing?”
“Sitting.”
“Mina.”
She had her hood off. Her hair was flat to her skull. She looked entirely calm and entirely somewhere else.

“You know what the actual number is, Cass? The one everybody gets wrong?” She wasn’t looking at me. She was looking at the horizon. “Dorian. Mavericks. Two waves on him, the worst hold-down in the recorded history of the sport, the one they made the vest because of. Sixty-eight seconds.”
“I know the number.”

“Everyone in that car park thinks they’ve done two minutes.” She finally turned her head. “Nobody has ever done two minutes here. Not once. Not in the whole history of this beach. The longest anyone has been under at this break and lived is about ninety.”
“Good,” I said.

“It’s not good, it’s nothing.” And there was heat in it, the first I’d ever heard from her. “Ninety seconds. That’s a bad phone call. That’s the length of a song intro. Whatever’s down there, nobody’s ever had time to look at it.”

The set came at seven minutes past three. She didn’t catch it. It landed on her about where I said it would and I had her out in twenty-six seconds, and she came up furious, not frightened, furious — spitting water and hammering the sled with the flat of her hand — and the thing I understood, sitting there with my hand on the throttle and her wrist in my other hand, is that she had not been trying to ride anything.
She’d been trying to get held under.
And the ocean, that day, hadn’t been generous enough.
ELEVEN. THE VESTIBULE
I went under on the twelfth of December at eleven-fifty in the morning and I was down for seventy-nine seconds, and this is the chapter I have been avoiding since I started.

It was my own fault and it was the stupidest possible mechanism. Not heroism. Not a rescue. I put the ski across the face of a wave I’d misread — the second of a four-wave set, which I had counted as the last of a three — and it picked the hull up and stood it on end and I went off the side into the pit with a two-hundred-and-ninety kilo machine somewhere above me.
I had no vest. Drivers don’t wear them. There isn’t room in the seat.
Zero to eight seconds.

Violence. That’s all. There’s nothing else in it and there’s nothing to learn from it. You are inside a washing machine the size of a church and you have no orientation whatsoever — not vague orientation, none, the concepts of up and down are simply withdrawn from you. You’re tumbled at a speed that pulls at the joints. My mask of air went instantly. Water in the sinuses, which burns like swallowing seawater through your face.

The one thing you do, the only thing, is cover your head with your arms and go loose. Rag-doll. Fighting costs oxygen and you have a fixed amount and you have just been informed that you will need all of it.
Eight to twenty-five.

The wave passes over and lets you go and you are now in the foam, and the foam will not carry you up. I clawed and got nothing. It’s like swimming in beer. You put your hand into it expecting resistance and your hand goes through and your body doesn’t move and there is a specific horror in that which I’ve never got out of my head — not the violence, the lack of purchase. The ocean stopped fighting me and simply declined to be pushed against.
Somewhere in there I hit the sand with my shoulder, which told me down, which was the first useful information I’d had.
Twenty-five to forty.
The contractions started.

I had done a hundred and forty pool sessions in that chair watching other people’s diaphragms fire and I had never once had a proper set of my own, and here is what nobody conveys: it does not feel like needing to breathe. Needing to breathe is a mild request you get after running for a bus. This is your torso being punched from the inside by something that is not you and does not care what you think. It came about every six seconds and each one folded me. My throat kept trying to open on its own. That’s the part I wasn’t ready for — the body attempting the swallow, again and again, the airway opening a fraction and my jaw clamping it, a negotiation happening in my neck between two systems that had never previously disagreed about anything.
This is the phase everyone means when they say I nearly died. Forty seconds in. Ninety-five percent of the oxygen still in the tank.
Forty to fifty-five.
Then something ended.
The contractions came further apart. Then further. Then stopped.
I want to be very careful here because this is the entire book.

They didn’t stop because I got better at it. They didn’t stop because I relaxed or found some technique or made peace with anything. They stopped because the level of carbon dioxide in my blood was no longer the loudest thing happening in my nervous system, and the reason for that is that my brain had begun to run short of oxygen and was, in the most literal sense, going quiet.
The alarm switched off. Because the building was on fire.
And the sensation of the alarm switching off, after fifty-five seconds of that, is the single most magnificent thing that has ever happened to me.
Fifty-five to seventy-nine.
It got warm.

Not metaphorically. The water at that beach in December is fourteen degrees and I have been cold in it for nine years and it got warm — a spreading, ordinary, bath-temperature warmth starting at the sternum and going outward through the shoulders. My hands stopped being my hands and became two things I owned somewhere.

The struggle was over. Not survived — over. Cancelled. And what came in behind it was not a feeling I had ever had access to, because I had spent forty-one years with an alarm running underneath every single second of my life and had never once heard the room without it.
It was quiet.

I have tried for a long time to find a better word. Quiet is what I’ve got. The absence of a noise I never knew was there. Every human being reading this is currently, right now, being nagged at a low level by their own chemistry — breathe, breathe, breathe, every four seconds, from birth, and you have never noticed it any more than you notice your own heartbeat.
Turn it off and there is space in you that you did not know was occupied.

I was not frightened. I want that on the record and I want it understood that this is not bravery, it is chemistry, it is what happens to any brain in that condition and it happened to me, a coward, a man who has never willingly gone under in his life.
The light was green-grey and coming down through about six metres of moving water in shafts, and the shafts were beautiful, and I remember thinking, with total lucidity, in a complete sentence:
Oh. This is what he was trying to tell me.
And then the visual field started to do something.

Not a hallucination. I need to be precise or the whole thing collapses into a ghost story. There was no room, no corridor, no figure, nothing you could photograph. What there was, was structure. The light stopped arriving as shafts and started arriving as edges — long straight boundaries meeting at consistent angles, above me and to the left, the way you’d perceive the corner of a large building through fog if you’d never seen a building and had no word for corner.

It had orientation. That’s what I can’t get past, sixteen months later, sitting here. It wasn’t everywhere. It was up and to the left, and it stayed there when I moved, which is not what shapes in your own eyes do.
I got very interested in it.

That’s the exact and honest description of the state I was in at seventy seconds under a collapsing sixty-foot wave with no air in my chest. Not terror. Not resignation. Interest. A calm, warm, unhurried curiosity about the thing up and to the left, and the beginnings of an intention to go and have a proper look.
There was no part of me at seventy-five seconds that wanted to surface.
None. Not a fragment. The idea of the surface had become a bureaucratic detail belonging to a person I’d stopped being.
Bruno Sá got me at seventy-nine.

He’d come off the cliff on the second ski when he saw mine go over. He found me by the fin of my own board, which was floating, because I’d cut nothing and had nothing to cut. He got a hand into the collar of my top and hauled and I came up through the foam.

I don’t remember the surface. I have no memory between the edges and lying on the sled with my cheek against wet pad while somebody shouted in Portuguese, and my hands were shaking with a fine fast tremor and my whole jaw was buzzing and I could not make my arms work.
That is called a samba, and I had watched it happen to other men more than a hundred times from a lifeguard chair, and I had thought it looked like the worst thing in the world.
From inside, it was the interruption.

They put me on the sand and Bruno was talking and a paramedic was doing something to my ear and none of it was reaching me, and about four metres away, at the top of the sand where the loose stuff starts, Renny Shaw stood with his hands in his fleece and a stopwatch in one of them, and he did not come over.
He waited until they’d got the blanket on me and the crowd had thinned.
Then he crouched down beside my head, and he did not ask if I was all right, and he did not ask what happened.
He said: “What did you see?”

And I heard myself, in a voice that was not steady, tell a fifty-eight-year-old ex-navy diving medic — a man I did not trust, in a car park, ninety seconds after the best experience of my life — about edges. Angles. Up and to the left.
Renny Shaw closed his eyes for a moment. When he opened them there was something in his face I’d never seen there and never saw again.
He said, “Which side of you was the beach?”
I had to think.
“Right,” I said. “The beach was on my right.”
And Renny said, very quietly, mostly to himself:
“Same as Ruy.”

Then he stood up, and wrote in the notebook, and walked back up the sand toward the car park, and I lay there in a foil blanket in the rain, forty-one years old, with the taste of the ocean in my sinuses and the first honest thought I’d had in nine years going through me like a spike.
I want to go back.
TWELVE. HERO MOMENT
Thursday the eighteenth was the one.

Buoy off the shelf reading eleven metres at twenty-one seconds at four in the morning, wind offshore at nine knots, tide filling to a high at eleven-forty. If you had asked any of the eighty people on that slipway to design the day themselves they would have designed that day and then apologised for being greedy.

Seventy-foot faces on the bigger sets. The lighthouse had four hundred people on it by eight. Three drone operators. A production truck from a streaming platform parked on the cliff road with a satellite dish folded on the roof like something praying.
Beto Krall had eleven content-eligible sessions logged and zero hero moments, and there were four weeks left in his contract year.
I knew that. I’d driven him to the meeting. I’d eaten the sardines.

I want to be honest about the fact that I did not think about it once that morning, because I was busy, and because if you spend nine years around men in that position you stop hearing it as information and start hearing it as weather.
At nine-twenty he asked me to drive him.

His usual partner was a Brazilian called Léo who was very good and who had a bad shoulder that week, and Beto came down the slip in his suit with his board under his arm and asked me, and I said yes, because I’m the best driver on that beach and because he asked me nicely and because I liked him, which I have not said yet in this book and should have.

I liked Beto Krall. He was not clever and he was not deep and he was enormously kind. He carried other people’s equipment without being asked. He learned enough Portuguese to talk to the widow who ran his guesthouse and he talked to her every single morning for two winters about her hip.
We ran three waves before eleven and all three were good and one was very good, and he came back to the ski each time with his eyes wide and his mouth open, laughing.
Then the set at eleven-ten.
I’ll do this cleanly. It doesn’t need decoration.
The set was four waves and the third was the biggest thing I had seen in nine years at that beach.

I had him at forty-five kilometres an hour on a good line and I put him in high, further up the face than I’d have liked, because that’s where the wave was and there was no negotiating with it. He let go of the handle clean. I banked off and got over the shoulder with maybe two seconds to spare, which is not enough, and I felt the ski go light underneath me at the top and come down hard in the flat behind.
I came around into the channel and turned and found him.

He was in the top third, high, and the wave had begun to do the thing this place does — the jack. The backwash came off the beach and met it and the whole face went from steep to past vertical, an overhang, seventy feet of water leaning out over the trough with a man standing on the underside of it.

He had a choice for about half a second. He could have straightened and gone for the flats and taken the whitewater on his back and been fine, and it would have been a nothing clip, a content-eligible session, one of eleven.
He turned up the face.

He put the board on its rail and cut back up into the pit, into the exact place where the lip was going to land, and he did it deliberately, and there are four separate camera angles of it and in every one of them the movement is unhurried.

The lip came over him as a slab, from a height of about six storeys, and it landed on him with the sound this coast makes twice a winter, and four hundred people on the cliff made a noise I still hear.
I opened the throttle before it finished falling.
Count.
Zero at impact. I was in the channel, seventy metres out, which is about eight seconds of hard running to get to the edge of the foam.
Eight: at the edge. The fourth wave of the set standing up behind me.

Eleven: I turned and took the fourth wave over the shoulder because going into the foam with that thing behind me would have made two casualties instead of one. Eleven seconds spent staying alive. There is no version of that decision I have found a way to regret and I have looked.

Twenty-four: back at the edge of the foam. The zone was a hundred and forty metres of white and the visibility across it was nothing at all — you are looking at a field of moving cream and there is a man somewhere in it and the only thing that will find him is his own vest.
Thirty-eight: nothing.
Fifty: I saw the board. Board first, always. Five metres of leash off it going down into the foam at an angle, taut, which meant he was on the end of it and the outflow had him.
Fifty-four: at the board. Knife off the mount, hand down the leash, cut. The leash went and the board went sideways.
Sixty-one: I had him.
Sixty-one seconds and I had my hand in the shoulder of Beto Krall’s vest and I hauled him across the sled, and his vest was not inflated.
He hadn’t pulled the cord.

Sixty-one seconds is seven seconds better than Dorian. Seven seconds inside the worst survived hold-down in the recorded history of the sport, and I did it in a hundred and forty metres of aerated foam with a fourth wave in the middle, and there is not one driver alive who would have done it faster.
