I want that written down because I have said it to myself roughly nine thousand times and it has never once helped.
He was blue at the lips and grey everywhere else and he was not shaking. That’s the thing. He wasn’t sambaing. The samba means the lights are flickering; no samba means the lights are off.

I got him to the sand in fifty seconds flat with the throttle wide open and the paramedics were already coming down and they worked on him on the beach for thirty-one minutes with four hundred people watching from a cliff and three drones overhead and one of the drones was livestreaming.
They got a rhythm back twice.
He died in the ambulance at the top of the hill without ever having been conscious, twenty-six years old, and his mother was in Curitiba and found out from a video.
The clip did eleven million in four days.

Eleven million. The turn back up into the pit, the slab coming over, the man deleted. It is, and everyone in the industry knows this and nobody says it, the best piece of big-wave footage ever captured, and it is on a hard drive in a production truck that drove off that cliff road on Friday morning and went to Lisbon.
Antonia sent a statement. The Head of Athlete Narrative posted a photograph of Beto laughing on a beach with the caption fly high brother and a wave emoji.
The energy drink with the lightning bolt going into a fist put out a two-minute tribute film eleven days later.
They did not take the wipeout down.

And on the sand, that afternoon, while the paramedics were packing up and the police were doing what police do and I was sitting on the wet with my back against the wall of the slip and my hands shaking so hard I couldn’t get the zip of my top down—
Renny Shaw came and crouched next to me. Same as before. Same crouch.
And he asked me the number.

Not are you all right. Not Christ, Cass. He asked me the number, and I told him — sixty-one — and he took out the black notebook and he wrote it down, and then he stood there with the pen on the page and did not close it, waiting.
Waiting for something else. Waiting for the other column.

And I understood, sitting in the wet sand watching a man hold a pen over a ruled line, that there was a box on that page which Beto Krall was never going to be able to fill in, and that Renny Shaw was, at that precise moment, upset about it.
Not about Beto.
About the box.
THIRTEEN. PADDLE OUT
They held it on the Sunday because the swell had dropped to eight feet and because Antonia’s people needed it to happen before the news cycle turned over.

I’m going to describe the memorial accurately and some people will find it disgusting. It was disgusting. It was also, in its way, the most honest thing that happened that entire winter, because at least nobody at that memorial pretended to be somewhere else.

A paddle-out is the surfing funeral. Everybody goes out past the break, forms a ring, holds hands, somebody says something, flowers go in the middle, everyone splashes water in the air and shouts. It’s genuinely old and it’s genuinely moving and I have been at four of them and cried at three.
This one had a call sheet.

An actual call sheet. Printed. I saw it in Antonia’s hand on the beach at nine-forty — 0955 ARRIVALS / 1015 CIRCLE FORMS / 1020 DRONE PASS A / 1024 FLOWERS. Two operators, because you need a second angle. A man from the streaming platform in a Patagonia jacket holding a clapperboard, which he tried to hide behind his leg when he saw me looking.
Ninety-one people paddled out for Beto Krall and I would put money on forty of them having met him.

The ring formed. Somebody said something in Portuguese that was kind and true. Léo, the Brazilian with the bad shoulder, wept openly with his face in his hands in the middle of the Atlantic and did not care who saw, and that was real, that was the realest thing in the water.

And then, while the flowers were still going in, a kid I didn’t know — twenty, maybe, Australian, a sticker on his board for a company that makes protein — turned to his mate about six feet from me and said, in a completely normal voice:
“Reckon they’ll re-run the Farol event or just call it?”
Here’s what they said at the bar afterwards, and I was there, and I’m putting it down.
That he was gone before he hit the water, which is not true, and which people say because it means nobody could have helped and therefore nobody failed.

That the vest failed. Also not true. The vest was found intact with the cartridge full and the pin unpunctured, which the sponsor knew by Saturday and did not correct, because the vest failed is a much better story for everyone than he didn’t pull it.
That the ocean chooses. Said twice, by two different men, both sober.
That he died doing what he loved. Said by me, nine years ago, on television, about my brother, so I kept my mouth shut.
And then Kirill Novak, four beers in, with his arm around a girl from the tourist office, said the thing that made me put my glass down and leave.
He said: “Sixty-one seconds, though. Sixty-one. That’s basically Dorian.” And he said it admiringly. He said it the way you’d say a lap time.

Nobody at that table corrected him. Nobody said and Dorian came up. Because it wasn’t a conversation about survival. It hadn’t been for years, and I was the only person in the room who still thought it was, and I was the guy with the boat.
I went and found Renny at eleven that night.
He was in the back room of the Baleia with tea, alone, with the notebook shut on the table under his hand.
“He didn’t pull the cord,” I said.
“I know.”
“You know.”
“The cartridge was full. Everyone knows, Cass, it’s a small town.”
I sat down opposite him and I put my hands flat on the table because otherwise I don’t know what they’d have done.
“Explain it to me.”
“Explain what?”

“A twenty-six-year-old with a functioning inflation vest and one pull available to him, on the end of a hold-down that had already gone past a minute, and he never reached across his own chest and pulled a toggle that was six inches from his hand.”
Renny turned the cup on the saucer.
“You’ve been under,” he said. “Nine days ago. Seventy-nine seconds. You tell me.”
And I sat there in a bar that smelled of wet coats and fried sardines with my hands flat on a table.
Because I knew.

I’d been there six days before Beto and I had lain in that green-grey light with the alarm switched off and the warmth coming through my shoulders and the edges up and to the left, and the surface had become a bureaucratic detail belonging to a person I’d stopped being. Those are my words from the chapter before this one. I wrote them before I wrote this, on purpose, so that you would already have them when you got here.
At seventy-five seconds I did not want to come up.

At sixty seconds, Beto Krall — who had done four years of tables, who could rock-run two lengths and part of a third, who had a hero-moment clause and a mother in Curitiba — got to the same place I’d got to, and it was calm and it was warm and the noise had stopped.
And a toggle on a cord is a piece of admin from the surface.
You don’t refuse it. That’s what people won’t understand. He didn’t heroically decline to save himself. He was somewhere that had no opinion about cords.
“He wasn’t drowning,” I said.
“No,” said Renny. “He was ninety seconds into being extremely happy, and then he stopped.”
I said the next thing carefully because I could feel the floor of my whole life shifting under it.
“You’ve got three others. Mina said. Three men who came up talking, last winter, off my sled. You’ve got what they said.”
“I’ve got what forty-one people said.”
“Forty-one.”

“Since 2009.” He drank his tea. “Nine of them from this beach. The rest from Mavericks, from Jaws, from two pools, from a decompression chamber in Faslane and from a man in a hospital bed in Portsmouth in 2011 who had been under a boat for four minutes.” He set the cup down. “Would you like to see it?”
Rain on the window. Cards in the front bar.
“Why now?”
And Renny Shaw looked at me with something that I have since decided was genuine, which is the part I’ve never made peace with.
“Because you’ve been in,” he said. “Until nine days ago you were an instrument. Now you’re a witness. I don’t share the ledger with instruments.”
I said: “What the fuck does that mean, an instrument.”
He picked up the notebook and put it in his fleece pocket and stood.
“Tomorrow,” he said. “Bring the log off your ski. The GPS one. All nine years of it.”

And he left, and I sat there for a long time, and it took me until about two in the morning — lying on my back in a flat above a garage, listening to the harbour wall knocking — to work out what a rescue-timing log has to do with anything, and when I did work it out I got up and was sick in the sink.
PROTOCOL II. THE RUNGS
This document does not exist. If you are reading it and you have not completed eighteen months of Table work, close it. You will hurt yourself and, worse, you will produce unusable reports.
PURPOSE. To arrive, observe, and return.

Everything in the published training is preparation for the first sixty seconds. The first sixty seconds are of no interest. They are the corridor you walk down to reach the door. Trainees become connoisseurs of the corridor and never open anything. This is the single most common failure and it is why the freediving federations, for all their instrumentation, have produced almost no usable material in forty years: they have optimised a sport around not going through.
THE LADDER.
Rung One — Struggle. Onset of diaphragmatic contraction. Thirty to sixty seconds for a trained subject in cold water at rest. Unpleasant, meaningless. No reports have ever come from Rung One.

Rung Two — Cessation. The contractions space out and stop. Subjects invariably describe this as mastery. It is not mastery. It is the beginning of oxygen deficit in the brain and the withdrawal of the warning system. Rung Two is the actual threshold. Everything before it is the queue.

Rung Three — Warmth and quiet. Peripheral sensation withdraws. Thermal misperception is near-universal — subjects in fourteen-degree water report bath temperature. Time perception loosens. Fear is absent. Not managed: absent. Reports from Rung Three are common and low-value. Subjects describe a feeling. Feelings are not data.

Rung Four — Structure. Onset variable; typically ninety to one hundred and thirty seconds by our timings, earlier under high cardiac load. Subjects report geometry. Edges, angles, boundaries, surfaces. Consistently oriented — that is, located in a stable position relative to the subject’s body, persisting through movement of the head and eyes. This is the finding. Everything else in this document is scaffolding for this paragraph.
Note carefully: at Rung Four the subject does not experience wonder. Wonder is a Rung Three artifact. At Rung Four subjects report interest. Several have used the word recognition.
Rung Five. We have four reports and three of them came from men who did not survive the week. I will not write down what is in them until the sample is larger.

PROCEDURE. Rungs Three and Four cannot be reached in a swimming pool. The heart rate is wrong, the cold is wrong, and no subject will voluntarily hold past Rung Two while a friend stands over him with a stopwatch. The body will not permit it. This is not cowardice, it is architecture: a conscious human being cannot override the airway indefinitely by decision alone.
Therefore the state requires an external agent to maintain the condition beyond the point of consent.
There is one available. It is free, it is enormous, and it does not negotiate.
The wave is not the objective. The wave is the only reliable apparatus on earth for holding a trained human being at Rung Four long enough to look at something.
RECORD-KEEPING. On surfacing the subject has approximately ninety seconds of accurate recall before confabulation begins. Do not ask what happened. Ask, in this order:
1. Which side of your body was the beach on? 2. Where was it? Give a direction relative to your own chest. 3. Did it move when you moved? 4. What was the temperature?
Never ask what it meant. The subject will tell you what it meant and everything after that sentence is worthless.

CONTRAINDICATION, ABSOLUTE. The inflation vest is not to be regarded as a safety device during a scheduled descent. It is a surface artifact. A subject at Rung Four who pulls the cord terminates a run that cost eighteen months to arrange.
A subject at Rung Four will not pull the cord.
We have never once needed to enforce this.
— R.S.
FOURTEEN. THE INSTRUMENT
He didn’t make me work for any of it. I want that clear, because I’ve told this wrong in my head a hundred times, in a version where I was clever.
I wasn’t clever. He told me. He sat me down in a garage with a heater and a folding table and he told me everything in about forty minutes, in order, the way you’d hand over a job.
The garage was under his flat on the Rua Nova. Concrete, one window, a workbench, a wall of shelves with box files on them going back years, all labelled in the same small hand.
He’d already got my ski log off the memory card and put it on a laptop, because I’d brought it, because he’d asked me to.
“Sit down. Do you want tea?”
“No.”
“Have tea.”
He made tea.
Then he turned the laptop round.

It was a scatter plot. I know what a scatter plot is. Horizontal axis was labelled T-DOWN, in seconds. Vertical axis was labelled something I didn’t understand and he explained in one sentence: the number of usable reports per run.
There were about four hundred dots.
Below sixty seconds on the horizontal, the dots sat on the floor. Nothing. A flat carpet of zeroes running along the bottom of the chart.
From about ninety onward, they climbed.
And there was a vertical dashed line at sixty-two seconds, drawn in, labelled in that small handwriting:
MOURA
“That’s your average,” Renny said. “Nine years. Four hundred and eleven recoveries. Sixty-two point four seconds from impact to hand-on-subject.”
I looked at it.
“That’s my job.”

“Yes,” he said. “It’s an extremely good average. It is, as far as I’m aware, the best working average on this coast by about nine seconds, and the second-best is a Hawaiian who only drives four days a year.”
“Then what’s the problem.”

“There’s no problem. It’s a very fine number.” He sat down opposite me with his own tea. “It’s just that it’s the wrong number, and you’ve been holding this beach to it since 2016, and nobody has ever been able to move you.”
Here is what he laid out, and he laid it out plainly, and none of it required me to work anything out.

Rung Four starts, on his timings, somewhere past ninety seconds. That’s where the geometry is. That’s where the reports come from, the ones that agree with each other, the ones with orientation in them.
I get to people at sixty-two.

So for nine years, every single time a rider on this beach went down and got somewhere interesting, a man on a jet ski arrived and took them out of it about thirty seconds early. Not once. Four hundred and eleven times.

“You’re the ceiling,” Renny said. “You are, functionally, the reason nothing has ever been observed properly at this break. There are two hundred kilometres of Portuguese coast producing the largest ridden waves on earth and the data is worthless, and the reason the data is worthless is that the best driver in Europe works here and he is very fast.”
He said it without accusation. That’s the part. There was no cruelty in it at all. He was describing a piece of equipment that was out of calibration.
“That’s what an instrument is,” I said.
“That’s what an instrument is.”
I said: “You could have just told me to go slower.”
“I did think about it.”
“And?”

“And you’d have said no.” He turned the laptop back round. “And then you’d have told the harbourmaster, and the crews, and there’d have been a great deal of noise, and I’d have moved to Ericeira and started again with a worse driver and it would have cost four years.”
“So instead you let me run at sixty-two and worked around me.”

“I worked with you. There’s a difference and it matters.” He tapped the dashed line on the screen. “Everything you’ve ever done has gone in the ledger. Your average is the most reliable variable on this coast. A subject who goes down here knows — not consciously, but the crews know, everyone knows — that there is a floor under them at roughly a minute. That floor is you.” He looked up. “Do you understand what that does?”
“No.”
“It lets them go further than they otherwise would.”
And I sat in a cold garage holding a mug of tea I didn’t want.
“I’m the reason they take the risk.”
“You’re the reason it’s affordable,” Renny said. “Yes.”
I asked him the obvious thing, and he answered it immediately, which is what I mean about him not hiding.
“Did anyone tell them? The riders. Do they know what you’re actually training them for?”

“Mina wrote it. She’s known since the second year. Kirill has never asked a question in his life and would not understand the answer. Iker knows and doesn’t care.” He drank his tea. “Beto knew. Beto knew completely, Cass, and he was better at it than anyone I have ever worked with, and he never once used a word like research. He called it Tuesdays.”
I thought of Beto rolling a cigarette badly in a truck outside a fish market.
It’s not even the worst part of my week.
“He wasn’t complaining,” I said.

“No. He was being modest.” Renny put his cup down. “It was the only part of his week that meant anything and he was slightly embarrassed about it, which is a very ordinary way for a young man to be about the most important thing in his life.”
And then he did the thing that I have never been able to file properly.

He got up, took a box file off the shelf — second from the left, third shelf, labelled in that small hand — and put it on the folding table in front of me, and opened it, and turned it round so it faced me the right way up.
Loose pages. Ruled columns, hand-drawn with a straight edge. The same layout as Mina’s, the same layout as the black notebook, going back and back.
The paper at the bottom of the stack was older. Different pen. A larger, looser, worse hand, with the letters leaning hard to the right and the ruling done freehand and crooked.
I knew it before I read a word of it, the way you know a voice through a wall.
Ruy wrote his sevens with a bar through them. Our mother taught us both and I never picked it up and he never dropped it.
Every seven on that page had a bar through it.
“Sit down,” Renny said, quite gently, because I hadn’t stood up, and then I did stand up, and the chair went over behind me and made a noise like a gunshot in that concrete room.

“He started it,” Renny said. “Not me. I want you to have that in the right order, because everything else in this room is mine and that isn’t. Your brother had been doing this for two years before he ever met me, on his own, badly, with a notebook from a supermarket, and he came and found me, at a conference in Lisbon, in 2015, because I’d published four pages on hypoxic phenomenology in 1998 that nobody else on earth had read.”
He straightened the chair I’d knocked over.
“I didn’t recruit your brother, Cass. Your brother recruited me.”
FIFTEEN. AGREEMENT

He read them to me out loud. That took about two hours and it was the strangest two hours of my life, a fifty-eight-year-old man in a fleece reading columns off loose paper in a garage while the rain came down outside and I sat there and did not once interrupt.
I’m going to give you a small part of it, in his order.
KN. Nazaré. Tow. 71 seconds. Warm. Not frightened. Something up and left, flat, big. Like being under a table.
I.A. Nazaré. Tow. 88. Ceiling on the left. Corner. Wanted to go to it.
M.S. Pool, weighted. 5:12. Above and left. Edges meeting. Two planes at an angle, could see the join. Not a wall — the outside of something.
R.M. Nazaré. Paddle. 94. Room. Big. Left side. Angle from below — like standing at the bottom of stairs looking up into a landing.
T.O. Mavericks. Tow. 77. Up and to the left, grey, straight lines. Was interested. Was not scared at all which I keep thinking about.
Faslane. Chamber. 4:40. Left. Structure. Corner of a large building.
Portsmouth. Under vessel. approx 4 min. A room above me and to my left. I was underneath it looking up.
Renny stopped and let the paper rest on his knee.

“Forty-one subjects,” he said. “Nine years. Eleven of them have never met each other and four of them are dead. Thirty-six of the forty-one place it in the upper left quadrant relative to their own chest. Twenty-nine use an architectural noun without prompting — room, ceiling, corner, wall, building, landing, stairs. Nineteen say not frightened unasked. Fourteen describe warmth in water below fifteen degrees.”
The heater ticked.
“That’s not a hallucination,” I said.

“It might be.” He said it flatly and immediately and it took the ground out from under me, because it was the last thing I expected him to say. “Cass, listen to me carefully, because this is where people go stupid and I’ve watched a lot of them do it. It might be entirely a hallucination. It very probably is.”
“But they agree.”

“Of course they agree.” He put the pages down. “Forty-one human brains, all of the same species, all built from the same instructions, all running out of the same fuel in roughly the same way. Why wouldn’t they produce the same picture? You put forty-one identical machines under identical stress and they fail identically. That’s not a discovery about the ocean. It’s a discovery about the machine.”
“Then what the hell are we doing?”

“Something extremely interesting either way.” He leaned forward. “Follow it through. If it’s the machine, then we have found a stable, reproducible perceptual state that the human brain enters under a specific chemical condition, which nobody has mapped, which shows up in a Scottish decompression chamber and a swimming pool and under a seventy-foot wave in Portugal, and which every single person who reaches it describes as the most significant thing that has ever happened to them.” He held up a hand. “That’s a finding. That’s a very large finding. It doesn’t need a single ghost in it.”
“And if it isn’t the machine?”
Renny Shaw looked at the window for a while.

“Then it’s the other thing,” he said, “and I’m not going to speculate in front of you, because you’re the only person in this story who’s entitled to an answer and I’m not going to hand you a guess dressed up as one.”
That’s the bit that got me. That’s the bit I keep coming back to.

He never once claimed. In three years I never heard that man make a supernatural claim, not one, not even drunk, and he didn’t drink. Every mystic I have ever met in this town was a twenty-four-year-old with a tattoo of a compass telling me the ocean had spoken to him. Renny Shaw had forty-one corroborating reports and a chart and he wouldn’t go one inch past what was on the paper.
It’s much, much harder to walk away from a man like that.
I asked him for Ruy’s.
He found it without looking, which meant he knew where it was, which meant he’d had it out recently.
Two pages. That crooked freehand ruling. The barred sevens.
The last entry in my brother’s handwriting was dated eleven days before he died and it wasn’t a report, it was a note to himself, and it said:
94 not enough. can see the join but not what’s past it. need to get properly held. tell C to stay in the channel.
I read it four times.
“Tell C to stay in the channel,” I said.
“Yes.”
“He was going to ask me to leave him under.”

“He never asked you,” Renny said. “You should hold onto that. He wrote it eleven days before and he never said it to you, and I’ve thought about why for nine years and the best I’ve got is that he couldn’t work out how to put it to his brother.” He took the page back, carefully, the way you’d take a photograph out of someone’s hand. “It’s the only decent thing in this entire box file, Cass. He knew what he wanted, he knew exactly who to ask, and he couldn’t make himself do it.”
I went out into the rain at about one in the morning and stood in the Rua Nova with my hands on my knees for a while.
Not because of the reports. Not because of the room, or the left side, or the corner of a large building.

Because for nine years I had been the man who got there in sixty-two seconds, and I had built an entire life on the sentence I was fast enough and it wasn’t enough, and I had been wrong about which word in that sentence was the problem.
I went back in. He was washing the mugs.
“When you asked me on the sand,” I said. “The day he died. Whether he was moving.”
“Yes.”
“Why did that matter?”

“Because if he was moving at sixty-two seconds,” Renny said, without turning round, “he was on Rung Three at most, and you took him out of the water in the middle of the safest part of the entire process, and he died of the pressure change on a fast ascent from six metres with a lung already loaded.” He put a mug on the rack. “He wasn’t dying when you got to him, Cass. He was fine. He was having the best minute of his life.”
The tap ran.

“You interrupted him,” Renny said, “and the interruption is what killed him. That’s not mysticism. That’s a pulmonary event with a mechanism you can read about in any diving medicine textbook, and it is the single most ordinary way to die in this sport, and everyone in this town thinks your brother drowned.”
He dried his hands.
“He didn’t drown. You brought him up too fast, because you loved him, and because you were nine seconds better than everybody else.”
SIXTEEN. NOTICE
I quit on the twenty-fourth of December by text message, which is a coward’s medium and was the correct one.
Not driving for the crew any more. Ski’s still available for the contest if the WSL want it, that’s between them and the harbourmaster. Don’t call me.
Renny replied in four minutes.
Understood. Thank you for nine years. The ledger will note the change.
Not one word of persuasion. That’s how you keep somebody — you let them go, cleanly, with a receipt.
I lasted six days.
What broke it was Iker.

The Basque kid. Nineteen years old, ninety kilos of nothing but shoulders, the one who’d asked me to take him back out instead of in. On the twenty-eighth, in a nothing swell, twenty-five-foot faces, absolutely routine — he went down on an inside section with two skis in the channel and neither of them was mine, because I was sitting in a flat above a garage with the curtains shut watching a Portuguese quiz show.
Nobody got to him for two minutes and ten seconds.

He’d gone down in a lull between waves, which meant no second wave, which meant no dragging, which meant that what happened to Iker was not a beating. It was just time. He was under, in one place, in ordinary green water eight metres deep, for a hundred and thirty seconds, and the drivers on that day were two Brazilians who were competent and who had never once in their lives had a reason to think the man they were looking for was anywhere other than the surface.
They found him at two-ten because he finally floated.
They brought him in on a sled and I got there because Bruno phoned me from the slip and I ran the whole way with my boots unlaced.
He was on the concrete by the fuel drums with four people round him.
He was sambaing.

I’d seen it a hundred and forty times from twelve feet up in a lifeguard chair and I had never once seen it from a metre away with a friend on the ground and here is what it actually is, and I’m going to write it properly because the rest of this book has been fairly clean and this part is not clean.

The whole body vibrates. Not a shiver — a buzz, four or five cycles a second, running through the trunk and out into the limbs, so that his heels drummed on the concrete in a fast irregular patter like something spilling. His hands were curled in and turned inward at the wrists, both of them, symmetrically, in a posture nobody adopts voluntarily. His jaw was going. His eyes were wide open and moving, and they were not tracking anything, they slid across my face and off it without the slightest change.

He was making a noise. That’s the part I hadn’t known about, because you can’t hear it from a chair. A soft rhythmic grunt on every fourth or fifth vibration, air being pushed out of a chest by the shaking rather than by intent. It sounded like a man being jostled in a queue.

There was foam at the corner of his mouth, pink-tinged, which is the lungs, which is fluid coming up because the alveoli have been squeezed and have started to leak — that’s the thing that killed my brother, that exact pink, and I have seen it twice in my life and both times it was on somebody I liked.

He’d wet himself. That’s normal. Nobody mentions it, ever, in any account of any of this, in nine years of bar talk I have never once heard it said out loud, and it happens most times, because the pelvic floor is muscle and the muscle has stopped receiving instructions.
Somebody had put a jacket over him. Somebody else was filming.
I got that phone and threw it into the harbour. It was an eight-hundred-euro phone and I have never been so calm about anything.

Then I knelt down on the concrete and put my hand flat on Iker’s sternum and waited, because there is nothing else to do — you keep the airway clear and you let it finish, and it finished at about forty seconds, and the buzz stopped all at once like a switch going, and the boy’s eyes came back on and found mine.

And Iker Aramendi, nineteen, lying in his own piss on a slipway with pink foam on his chin, looked at me with total clarity and said the first thing that came into his head, which is what they all do, which is why the ninety seconds after matters more than any interview ever conducted.
He said, in English, because I don’t speak Basque and he was being polite even then:
“It’s much better further in.”
Then he cried for about a minute. Then he asked for his phone.

Renny had the recorder going. He’d been standing four metres back the entire time with a small grey digital recorder held at chest height and he had not moved to help, because there was nothing useful he could do and because there was something useful he could do and he was doing it.
I stood up.

I want to say I hit him. I’ve imagined it enough. I stood on that slipway with wet knees and a dead phone in the harbour and I looked at a fifty-eight-year-old man holding a recorder and I understood two things at once, which is the worst kind of understanding.

The first was that Renny Shaw had just recorded the cleanest Rung Four report of the entire nine years, on land, from a conscious subject, ninety seconds after surfacing, unprompted, with four witnesses.

The second was that if I had been in the water Iker would have been out at sixty-two seconds and would have said nothing at all, and would have gone home, and would have come back in March and done it again with less information.
“Two-ten,” Renny said. “Do you want to know the last time this beach produced a two-ten that lived?”
“No.”
“Never,” he said. “Not once. You’ve been here nine years.”
He put the recorder in his fleece.

“He’s fine,” Renny said. “He’ll have a headache and a cough for three days and his chest will hurt when he laughs. He was never in danger of dying, Cass, he was in danger of being interrupted, and today nobody interrupted him and now we have the best single line in the file.”
It’s much better further in.
I went back on the second of January.

Not for Renny. I want that on the page even though I’m aware of exactly how it reads. I went back because the alternative was sitting in a flat with the curtains shut while nineteen-year-olds went down in front of drivers who thought two minutes was a tragedy, and because I had spent nine years being the fastest man on that coast and the only thing I had ever actually done with it was pull my brother out of the best minute of his life.
Renny didn’t say anything when I came down the slip. He didn’t smile. He handed me a fuel can, which is the most tactful thing anyone has ever done for me.
And that night he sent one message.
Contest window opens the 14th. Models are showing something behind it. If it comes in as forecast it will be the largest swell recorded at this beach.
I’d like you to run the count as normal. Nothing changes. You do your job.
— R.S.
Nothing changes. You do your job.
I read that about nine times, looking for the trap, and there wasn’t one, and that’s because the trap was that there wasn’t one.
He didn’t need me to go slower any more.
He’d worked out that if the swell was big enough, I wouldn’t be able to get there.
END OF PART TWO
III. THE GLORY
SEVENTEEN. GREEN LIGHT
The call went out at 06:40 on the eleventh of January for a contest window opening on the fourteenth, and by lunchtime there were eleven thousand people booked into a town with four thousand beds.
I’ll do the swell properly one more time, because this is the one, and because everything in this book has been building toward a set of numbers that I still don’t entirely believe I watched arrive.

A low pressure system formed south of Greenland on the seventh at 962 millibars, which is a serious storm and not an unusual one. On the eighth it stalled — it stopped moving forward and sat, spinning, over the same patch of North Atlantic for thirty-one hours, with a fetch of eleven hundred kilometres of open water and sustained winds of ninety knots blowing in one consistent direction along the whole length of it.

That’s the recipe. Not violence. Duration and alignment. A storm that sits still and blows the same way for a day and a half organises the sea underneath it into something that stops being chop and starts being a machine.
By the ninth it was throwing swell. By the tenth the deep-water buoys west of Ireland were reading sixteen metres significant height at twenty-four seconds.

Twenty-four seconds. I said earlier that twenty-two is a phone call at four in the morning. Twenty-four is something else. At that period the energy is running four hundred metres deep and moving at about seventy kilometres an hour across the open ocean and it will lose almost nothing between Ireland and here.
And it was going to arrive, on the models, at high tide on the fifteenth, with the wind offshore at eight knots.
Every man in that bar knew what that meant and not one of them said it out loud, which is the same thing as everyone saying it.

The town in the four days before a swell like that is not a party. That’s the mistake people make from the outside. There’s no atmosphere. What there is, is logistics, and logistics performed by frightened people has a particular quality to it, a sort of over-carefulness, like the morning of a funeral.

The GNR closed the cliff road to private vehicles on the thirteenth. The council brought in six portable toilets and a barrier system and an ambulance that parked at the top of the slip and stayed there for a week with two paramedics in it playing cards.
The lighthouse sold out its viewing platform. Actually sold out, an actual ticket, eleven euros.
A helicopter came from Lisbon on the fourteenth and did a loop and went away and came back the next morning and stayed.
Nineteen skis registered with the harbourmaster. Nineteen. I have never seen more than eleven at that break in my life.

And in among all of it, in a rented flat above a garage, a fifty-eight-year-old man with a folding table and a box file was, I am absolutely certain, doing arithmetic about how long a human being could be held under seventy feet of water while nineteen drivers failed to find him.
I went to see Mina on the thirteenth.
She was packing her flat. Not moving out — packing the way you pack when you’re being careful, boxes labelled, the wetsuits off the hooks and rolled.
“You’re leaving?”
“No.” She taped a box. “I’m tidying. If it goes wrong I’d rather my mother didn’t have to sort through a shithole.”
Said absolutely flatly, without any drama in it at all, and she went on taping.
I sat down on the second chair, which was empty now, because the ledger was gone from it.
“Renny’s got you on something.”

“Renny hasn’t got me on anything. I’ve got me on something.” She looked up. “This is the difference you can’t seem to hold in your head, Cass, and it’s honestly starting to bore me. Nobody’s making me. There’s no gun. I’ve wanted to see the join for four years and on Thursday morning the largest wave ever recorded at this beach is going to arrive and hold me down for as long as I can arrange to be held down, and I have thought about it every day since I was twenty-six, and it is mine.”
“It killed Beto.”
“Beto was interrupted.”
“He was sixty-one seconds under with a full cartridge—”

“—and he didn’t pull it, and you know exactly why he didn’t pull it, because you were there eight days before him and you didn’t want to come up either.” She set the tape down. “You’ve been under once, for seventy-nine seconds, and you came back and you’ve spent a month being angry at everyone in this town for wanting the thing you want.”
The pigeons went off downstairs.
“That’s not fair,” I said.

“It’s completely fair. It’s the only thing I’ve said to you in three years that’s completely fair.” She went back to the box. “You want to go under. You’ve wanted it since Ruy. The only difference between you and me is that I’ve been honest about the arrangements.”
At the door — and this is the last conversation I ever had with her in that flat, so I’ve kept it exactly — I asked her the question I’d been carrying since the garage.
“If it’s just brains. If Renny’s right and it’s forty-one machines failing the same way and there’s nothing down there at all. Does that change it?”
Mina Sadr stood in her doorway with a roll of packing tape in her hand and thought about it seriously, for about eight seconds, the way she thought about everything.
“No,” she said.
“Why not?”

“Because either way it’s the only place a person is ever completely quiet,” she said, “and I’d like to go and look at it properly before I die, and I don’t much care whether it’s a room or a mistake.”
She shut the door gently. Same as the first time.
Two days later the swell hit the outer buoy at twenty-four seconds and the whole coast started to shake.
PROTOCOL III. SURRENDER
Final instruction. Nothing follows this one.
PURPOSE. To remain.

Everything you have trained until now has been resistance — tolerating, enduring, holding on. That was scaffolding and you may now take it down. What is required at the end is the opposite skill and it cannot be practised in a pool, because a pool has never once tried to kill anybody.
THE INSTRUCTION. When the wave takes you: do nothing.
Not relax, which is a word people say and mean nothing by. Do nothing. Do not orient. Do not locate the surface. Do not swim, kick, reach, or arrange your limbs. Do not decide anything at all.

Rag doll is the surfers’ word for it and they use it with contempt, as an insult, to describe a man being thrown about — and that contempt is the last piece of stupidity you will have to put down. Total passivity is not the failure state. It is the technique. It is, in oxygen terms, the difference between ninety seconds and a hundred and forty.
A struggling man burns his reserve in the first thirty seconds and arrives at the door with nothing left to look with.

COSTS, IN ORDER OF EXPENSE. Fear is the most expensive thing you can do underwater. It is not an emotion down there, it is a fuel rate. A frightened heart at a hundred and forty beats will consume in forty seconds what a calm heart at fifty consumes in two minutes. Swimming is second. Deciding is third and is the one nobody warns you about. Cognition costs. Any man who spends the descent thinking about his wife will not see anything.

WHAT TO EXPECT AT THE TRANSITION. The contractions cease. This is Rung Two and it is the last honest signal your body will ever give you. Everything after it, you have been warned, is happening in a brain that is running down.
Proceed anyway.

WHAT NOT TO DO ON ARRIVAL. Do not attempt to approach it. Subjects at Rung Four consistently report an intention to move toward the structure. Do not. There is nowhere to go, you are inside a collapsing wave, and the impulse to travel is the one thing at that depth that will spend what little you have left.
Look. Note which side. Note whether it moves when you move.
Then come back and tell somebody.
ON RETURNING. You will not want to. I have been told this by every subject who has been past Rung Three and I have never once been told the opposite.
The reluctance is not a symptom of danger. It is an accurate response to where you are and what you have found, and I am not going to insult you by calling it confusion.
You will come back anyway. Not because you want to. Because somebody arranged for you to be able to, and that arrangement was expensive, and other people are waiting for the report.

A NOTE, WHICH IS NOT PROCEDURE. I have spent twenty-two years sitting outside chambers and thirty years reading files and I have never been in. I never will. My chest went in 1997 and there is no version of this in which I get to see it.
Forty-one of you have. Three of you did not come back and I have their pages and I read them more than is good for me.

Whatever it is — the room, the corner, the join, the outside of something — you are the only people who have ever stood in front of it, and every one of you got there on one breath, with nothing, in the dark, with no instrument but your own body.
Do not let anyone tell you it was a symptom.
Go and look. Then come back.
— R.S.
EIGHTEEN. FIFTEENTH
It came in overnight and by four in the morning nobody in that town was asleep, because you couldn’t be.
I’ve told you about the sound already. Forget it. That was a different animal.

What arrived on the fifteenth of January did not make a noise you could locate. There was no crash and no bang and nothing you could point at. There was a continuous low pressure in the air, a sort of standing rumble underneath everything, and every forty seconds it would swell up into something enormous and then subside, and the windows in my flat moved in their frames each time, and a glass on the drainer walked eleven centimetres across the steel over the course of the night and I watched it do it.
Dogs went mad in the old town. That’s documented, that’s in the newspaper. Every dog in Nazaré barked from about one in the morning.

I got down to the slip at five-forty in the dark and there were already four hundred people on the cliff road walking up in the rain with torches, like a pilgrimage, which is exactly what it was and everyone would have been offended by the word.
First light at seven-fifty.

I have driven at this beach for nine years and I have seen it at seventy feet and I want to be extremely careful here because this is the only paragraph in the book where I am at risk of sounding like the men in the bar.
The sets were coming in at eleven-minute intervals in groups of four to six.
The faces on the third and fourth waves of the bigger sets were somewhere between ninety and a hundred feet.

That’s not my measurement. I don’t measure. Three separate outfits with calibrated equipment and drone telemetry put the largest faces of that morning between twenty-seven and thirty-one metres, and the argument about the exact figure went on for fourteen months and was still going on when I started writing this, and the reason it went on is the reason everything about that place goes on: nobody can measure them properly. They put a man on a face and count him as a unit of height. The wave arrives, breaks in eleven seconds, and never exists again. There is no rewinding it, no second attempt, no laboratory. The largest thing that has ever happened at this beach is an event with no witnesses that agree.
Ninety feet is nine storeys.
I want to try one image and then I’ll stop.

When a wave of that size stands up and goes vertical, there is a moment — about a second and a half — where the face is not moving toward you, it’s just standing there, and the water on it is running upward. Upward. The surface of a nine-storey wall of water climbing toward the sky. And in that second and a half the whole thing goes translucent at the top where the sun’s behind it, so you can see the shadows of the swell behind it through it, and there are birds in front of it that are the size of specks of dirt.
Then the top third comes off.

It doesn’t curl. Curling is a small-wave word. It comes off as a slab about eight metres thick and the length of a football pitch and it falls, in the way that a building falls, with that same wrongness of scale where the eye insists it’s slower than it is.
When it lands, the water it displaces goes up. A wall of white goes forty, fifty feet into the air along the whole line of impact and stands there for a second before the wind takes it flat.
That’s what these people had been training for four years to be underneath.
The contest was called off at eight-fifteen.

Of course it was. Nobody says this part but it’s the most important administrative fact of that entire day: it was too big to compete. The event needs a jury to score rides and skis to rotate and a safety plan that a lawyer has signed, and at ninety feet the safety plan is a work of fiction. The head judge came on the radio and called it and there was no argument from anybody.

Which meant that from eight-fifteen onward, the largest swell ever recorded at that break was breaking on an empty ocean, in front of eleven thousand people, with no contest, no scores, no prize money and no rules.
A free session.
You have never seen anything like what that does to men.
Within forty minutes there were nine skis in the water and none of them had permission to be there.
I sat in the channel with the engine idling and did the only useful thing available, which was to count skis and note who was riding.
Kirill went out at eight-fifty with a Portuguese driver and got a good one and came back howling.
Léo went. Bruno went. Two Brazilians I didn’t know. A South African woman called Dee who I’d pulled twice and liked enormously and who rode with more sense than anyone on that beach.

Renny came down the slip at nine with the Napat on its trailer and did not put it in the water. He backed it to the top of the concrete, set the chocks, and stood next to it with the notebook in his fleece and a pair of binoculars, and he stayed in that exact position for the next four hours and did not move except to write.
And Mina Sadr came down at nine-twenty in a suit with no logos on it, carrying a board with no logos on it, and walked past me on the slip without stopping and said one thing.
“Left of the peak. Whatever happens. Stay left of the peak.”
That’s a place. Left of the peak, off the shoulder, is a hundred and twenty metres from where the impact zone actually is on a day like that.
She was telling me where to be so that I would be too far away.

She was being kind. That’s the thing I understood as she walked past — she was doing me a kindness, taking the decision off me in advance, giving me a place to stand where nobody could later say I should have gone.
I said her name.
She kept walking.
NINETEEN. MINA’S WAVE
She went at eleven-forty on the fourth wave of the biggest set of the day, and Léo drove her, and he drove her perfectly, and he has never once ridden since.
I was left of the peak.

I was where she told me to be, a hundred and twenty metres off, with the engine idling and my hand on the throttle and a knife on the mount, and I could see everything and reach nothing, which was the arrangement, which she had made for me as a gift.

The set showed at eleven-thirty-one. You see them a long way out on a day like that — four dark lines on the horizon that are not moving in any way you can perceive, and then two minutes later they have doubled in height and are still not visibly moving, and then they are on top of the canyon.
The first two went unridden. The third had a Brazilian on it who kicked out early.
The fourth stood up out of the deep and kept standing.

Léo had her at fifty kilometres an hour on a long line coming down off the shoulder. He put her in high and late — later than anyone would have chosen, later than I’d have gone — and he did that because she asked him to, and I know that because he told the inquiry and because he has said it out loud in a bar exactly once, to me, in April, weeping.
She let go of the rope.

And then Mina Sadr rode about eleven seconds of the largest wave I have ever seen a human being on, and she did it beautifully, and I need you to know that, because everything after this is horror and I refuse to let the horror eat the eleven seconds.

She was on a face somewhere near ninety feet. Her line was low and clean and fast, a long diagonal running ahead of a lip that was coming over the whole length of the wave behind her like a roof being pushed off a terrace. She went past the peak. She went past the section that had eaten Beto in December. Twenty thousand tonnes of water falling over behind her shoulder and she was ahead of it and pulling away and the cliff was making a noise I could hear over the engine at a hundred and twenty metres.
She had it.

That’s the part nobody accepts. She had made it. Another four seconds on that line and she was out into the flats and it would have been the biggest wave ever ridden by a woman and possibly by anybody and there would have been a Guinness certificate and a documentary and a life.
At second eleven she straightened her board.
Turned it, deliberately, ninety degrees, up the face, into the pit.
Same movement Beto made in December. Unhurried.

She had planned it, she had arranged her driver and her position and her ski and the man watching from a hundred and twenty metres, and she had trained four years for it, and she went up into the falling lip of a ninety-foot wave on purpose in front of eleven thousand people and a helicopter.
The wave took her at eleven-forty-one and eighteen seconds.
I started my count.
Twenty seconds. The wave finished breaking. The whitewater from the impact went up fifty feet and stood there and blew flat. Léo’s ski was inside and I could see him already turning.
Forty seconds. Nothing. That’s normal. Forty is nothing.

Fifty-five. The fifth wave of the set landed on the same water. Léo had to run. I opened my throttle and came in ten metres and stopped, because in front of me was a field of white that was two hundred metres across and I could not have kept a hull on it.
Seventy. Léo was in the outer foam. Bruno was coming from the north. Two other skis converging. Four drivers on the best day of their lives and none of us could get into the middle of it.
Ninety. This is where the count usually ends. Ninety is a long hold-down. Ninety is a story you tell.
Two minutes.
I want to describe two minutes.

Two minutes is a hundred and twenty individual seconds and I counted every one of them out loud, alone, on an idling jet ski, and I have never in my life experienced duration the way I experienced it between ninety seconds and two minutes on the fifteenth of January.
The helicopter was overhead. The cliff had gone quiet — eleven thousand people, silent, which is a sound of its own. Somebody on the radio was saying a name over and over.
Two-ten. That’s Iker. That’s the number that came up talking.
Two-thirty.
At two-thirty I went in.

I put a two-hundred-and-ninety kilo ski into two hundred metres of aerated foam on a day with ninety-foot sets running at eleven-minute intervals, which is the stupidest thing I have ever done and which every driver on that beach did within forty seconds of each other, all four of us, without a word on the radio.

The hull dropped. That’s what it does in that stuff — there’s nothing to plane on, it just sinks in and slews. I went fifteen metres and the ski went over and I came off and I was in it, in the white, and I could not see the surface because I was on the surface and it looked exactly the same as everything else.
Bruno got me. Bruno got me. That’s the day I had.
Three minutes.
Three-forty.

At three-forty the sixth set of the morning showed on the horizon and the GNR came on the radio and ordered every ski out of the zone, and Bruno had my collar and was shouting at me in Portuguese, and I was shouting nothing, because I had stopped counting at three-forty-one, and I don’t know why that number, and I have never started again.
They found her at four fifty-eight in the afternoon, five hundred metres north, in the rocks under the cliff.
The vest was inflated.
That’s the detail. Out of everything, that’s the one I’ve never been able to put down.

Her cartridge was empty and both bladders were full and her hand was still through the loop of the toggle cord, and the coroner’s report notes it in a single line in the equipment section, and it means one thing, which is that at some point down there, in the dark, at some depth, at some number of seconds, in the warm and the quiet with the edges up and to the left—
Mina Sadr changed her mind.
She wanted to come back.
And it was too late by then, because the vest lifts you at a speed you don’t control, and she came up under a set, and the pressure change did to her what it did to my brother.
She pulled the cord.
She fucking pulled it, and it killed her, and if she’d left it alone she might have floated up slowly in eleven minutes and been alive.
I sat on the concrete at the top of the slipway for a long time that evening after they took her up.

Renny Shaw came and stood next to me. Not crouched. Stood, with the binoculars still round his neck and the notebook shut in his hand, and he looked at the water for a while, and he was, I could see, absolutely wrecked. His face had come apart. He’d known her nine years.
I said: “She pulled it.”
“I know.”
“You wrote in that book that a subject at Rung Four doesn’t pull the cord. You wrote we have never once needed to enforce this.”
“I know what I wrote.”
“So she got somewhere you’ve never had a report from,” I said, “and the first thing she did was try to get out.”
And Renny Shaw stood on that slipway with eleven thousand people filing back down the cliff road behind us and said, very quietly:
“Yes.”
Then he said: “I need to make a call.”

And he walked up the hill with his phone already in his hand, and that was the moment — that, right there, not the ledger, not the chart, not the garage — that was the moment I understood I had never once asked who was paying for the swimming pool.
TWENTY. THE CLIENT
I found out on the twenty-ninth of January, in the garage, and once again nobody made me work for it, and once again that was the worst part.

I went round there to ask him to stop. That’s genuinely what I went for. Two dead in six weeks, one of them the best person in the whole enterprise, and I went up the Rua Nova at nine in the evening to ask a fifty-eight-year-old man to shut it down.
He was packing box files into crates.
Not hiding them. Packing them, methodically, with foam sheeting between the layers, and a printed manifest on the workbench with numbers against each box.
“You’re leaving.”
“The material is.” He didn’t stop working. “I’m going to Basel on the eleventh.”
“What’s in Basel?”
And Renny Shaw straightened up, and put his hands on the small of his back the way older men do, and said:
“The client.”
He made tea. Of course he made tea.
“You’ve never asked,” he said, “in three years, who pays for the pool.”
“I assumed you did.”

“On a navy pension.” He handed me the mug. “Two hundred a session for you, three-fifty for the pool hire, the boat fuel, the recorders, four thousand a year in insurance for a training operation that officially doesn’t exist. Eleven thousand euros a year, Cass, minimum, for nine years, out of a man with no income.”
I sat down on the folding chair.
“Who.”

“A company. You won’t have heard of it and I’m not going to give you the name, because you’ll go and shout at a receptionist in Switzerland and it’ll achieve nothing.” He sat down opposite. “Neuropharmaceutical. Mid-size. Two hundred and eleven employees. They have a division that works on what’s called state induction — pharmacological reproduction of specific, defined conscious states. It’s a real field. It’s been a real field since the Sixties and it got serious money again about a decade ago.”
“And they’ve been funding this.”

“They’ve been funding me. Since 2017.” He drank his tea. “The formal arrangement is a consultancy. I supply structured phenomenological reports from subjects in acute hypoxia, with physiological correlates where available, indexed by depth of deficit and duration. Forty-one subjects. Four hundred and ninety-two individual runs.”
“Say it in English.”
“They’re paying me for what people see,” Renny said, “when they nearly die.”

I want to lay out what he told me next as plainly as he told it to me, because when I’ve tried to explain it since, people always assume I’m being hysterical, and I’m not, and the thing itself is quite dull, which is why it works.

The problem in that industry, he said, is not making drugs. Making drugs is easy. The problem is targets. You cannot chemically reproduce a state unless you can first define the state — describe it precisely enough, and consistently enough across independent subjects, that you can say what you’re aiming at and know when you’ve hit it. A feeling isn’t a target. “Bliss” isn’t a target. Nobody can build toward a poem.

What is a target: a state that thirty-six out of forty-one independent subjects describe using the same spatial orientation, the same architectural vocabulary, the same absence of fear, the same thermal misperception, arrived at through the same chemical route, reproducibly, on demand.
That’s not a poem. That’s a specification.

“Rung Four is the most consistently reported non-ordinary conscious state in the literature,” Renny said. “By a distance. Nothing in the psychedelic corpus is that stable — you give forty people the same dose of the same compound and you get forty different countries. Hypoxia gives you the same building. Every time. In a pool in Portugal and a chamber in Faslane and under a boat in Portsmouth.”
“Because it’s the machine failing,” I said. “You told me that. Forty-one identical machines failing identically.”
“Yes.” He looked at me steadily. “And a fault that reproduces perfectly in every unit is not a fault, commercially. It’s a feature with a known trigger.”
I asked how much.
He told me, immediately, without any shame at all, which I’ve thought about a lot.

Eleven thousand a year in operating costs, covered. A consultancy fee of sixty thousand a year to him personally, paid through a company in Dublin. And a milestone payment, contingent on delivery of a validated corpus of one hundred and fifty subject-runs at Rung Four or deeper with physiological telemetry.
Four hundred thousand euros.
“Have you delivered it?”

“Four hundred and ninety-two runs, but only a hundred and forty-nine at Rung Four or deeper with usable telemetry.” He turned the cup on the workbench. “Mina’s was the hundred and fiftieth. She was wearing a logging oximeter under the sleeve of her suit and it recorded continuously for eleven minutes and it was on her body when they found her at the rocks and the data is intact.”
The heater ticked.
“You’ve got her blood oxygen,” I said. “Second by second. All the way down.”
“Yes.”
“For three and a half minutes past anything anyone’s ever recorded.”
“Yes.”
“A hundred and forty-nine,” I said. “That’s what you had on the fourteenth of January.”
“Yes.”
“So she’s the one that finishes the contract.”
“Yes.”
“Renny.” My voice had gone somewhere strange. “That’s the most valuable thing in the entire nine years.”

“It’s the most valuable thing in the field,” he said. “There is no other trace like it anywhere on earth and there never will be, because no ethics committee in the world will ever approve an experiment that produces one.”
And then Renny Shaw put his tea down and said the sentence that I have not got out from under, and I don’t think I will:
“She knew that. She put it on herself that morning. She checked the battery in front of me on the slipway at nine-fifteen.”
I said: what’s the product.

He got a folder off the bench and opened it and turned it round to face me, the way he’d turned the box file round in December, and it was a slide deck. An actual corporate slide deck, printed, spiral bound, forty pages.
The working name on the front was a string of letters and a number.

Inside, on slide nine, was a paragraph in ordinary business English describing the target profile of a compound in preclinical development, and I read it about six times, and here is what it said, in summary, in my words, because I’m not going to reproduce their sentences.
Fifteen minutes.
Sublingual. At home. No supervision required.

A reproducible state of absolute anxiolysis — that’s the word, it means the total absence of anxiety — with mild thermal warmth, temporal dilation, and stable, benign spatial hallucinosis. No respiratory involvement. No hypoxia. No risk.
Onset four minutes. Duration fifteen. Full recall. Drive an hour later.
Projected pricing, on a subscription model, at somewhere around the cost of a phone contract.
I sat in a cold garage in a fishing town holding a spiral-bound document and I laughed, out loud, once, and it came out of me like something breaking.
Because here’s the thing. Here’s the whole obscene shape of it.
Ruy trained for two years on his own with a supermarket notebook and drowned at twenty-six on a Tuesday in February.
Beto did four years of Tuesdays and turned back into the pit at seventy feet with a full cartridge and left a mother in Curitiba to find out from a video.
Iker went down for two minutes and ten seconds in front of two competent Brazilians and came up and pissed himself on a slipway and said it’s much better further in.
Mina Sadr gave four years and a life and three and a half minutes of the cleanest telemetry ever recorded to get properly held for the first time in human history.

And on slide nine of a spiral-bound folder, the thing they went down there for was available in fifteen minutes, with no ordeal attached, for about the price of a phone contract, and you could drive afterwards.

Everything. Every single thing. The cold, the tables, the lead, the fear, the two hundred metres of foam, the pink at the corner of the mouth, the wet trousers, the four hundred and eleven times I got there in sixty-two seconds — all of it, the entire cost of the entire enterprise —
— was market research.
“You knew,” I said. “The whole time. When you were reading me those reports in this room and saying you wouldn’t speculate. When you told me it was a finding and it didn’t need a ghost in it.”
“All of that was true.”
“You were sourcing.”

“Yes,” said Renny Shaw. “Both. That’s the part you’re going to have to sit with, Cass, and I’ll save you a year: it’s both, and neither one cancels the other. I believe every word I’ve ever said to you about what’s down there. I have also been paid sixty thousand euros a year to write it down in a format that a company in Basel can use.”
He closed the folder.
“I’d have done it for nothing,” he said. “Nobody offered me nothing.”
TWENTY-ONE. SLIDE THIRTY-ONE

I took the deck. He let me. He didn’t even watch me do it — he went on packing crates while I sat on a folding chair in a cold garage and read forty pages of a document that was never meant to be read by anybody who had touched saltwater.

Most of it was what you’d expect. Market sizing. A competitor landscape with names in it I recognised from television advertisements. Regulatory pathway. A chart projecting something called addressable anxiety burden across four territories.
Slide twenty-two was headed CONSUMER INSIGHT —
QUALITATIVE.
It was six quotes in a nice sans-serif font with the corporate blue underneath them, arranged in two columns of three, the way they teach you to lay out testimonials.
They were from the ledger.
Warm. Not frightened.
Above and left. Edges meeting.
It’s much better further in.

Iker Aramendi, nineteen years old, lying in his own piss on a slipway with pink foam on his chin, ninety seconds after the longest survived hold-down in the history of that beach, saying the truest thing anyone said in the entire nine years —
— set in eleven-point type, in a column, as consumer insight.
There was a caption underneath the six of them, in italics.
Subject reports, unprompted, post-event (n=41).
I got to slide thirty-one at about eleven at night.
It was headed BRAND TERRITORY, and it was mostly white space, because that’s how they signal that something is important.

In the middle, in large type, was a phrase they were considering as a name for the state itself. Not the compound — the compound had a code. This was the word the customer would use. The thing you’d say to your friend at work. Six letters.
And underneath it, in smaller type, in quotation marks, attributed to nothing and nobody, with no source line, no citation, no name:
“There’s a room down there.”
I have never told anyone what my brother said on the sand. I said that in the third chapter of this book and it was true when I wrote it and it is still true.
Two paramedics heard it and thought it was hypoxia. A cameraman was rewinding. My mother was not there. I have never said it out loud to another human being in nine years.
Except once.

In a garage, in December, to a man who asked me what did you see, and then asked me which side was the beach on, and then said same as Ruy, and I had thought at the time — I had genuinely thought — that he was telling me something kind.

He’d had it from Ruy directly. Of course he had. Ruy went to Lisbon in 2015 and found him and gave him everything, the notebook, the sevens with the bars through them, the whole two years of it, and somewhere in that handover my brother told a stranger the thing he would say again eleven months later lying on his back on wet sand with the ocean running off him.
And it had gone in the ledger.
And the ledger had gone to Basel.

And on slide thirty-one of a spiral-bound folder, in quotation marks, with no name attached, was the last coherent sentence my brother ever spoke, being considered as brand territory for a subscription product.
I put the deck down on the folding table and I sat there for a while.

Renny had stopped packing. He was standing by the crates with a roll of foam sheeting in his hand, watching me, and he had understood exactly which page I was on, because he’d been waiting for it, because he knew the deck by heart and he knew what was on thirty-one and he had handed it to me anyway.
“You could have taken that out,” I said.
“I didn’t put it in.”
“You gave it to them.”

“I gave them four hundred and ninety-two reports, and a company in Basel with a marketing function went through them and chose the best line, and the best line was your brother’s, because your brother was better at this than anybody who has ever done it.” He set the foam down. “He was twenty-six and he had no training and no equipment and no vocabulary and he came up out of sixty-two seconds and produced the single most usable sentence in the entire corpus. Six words. Nobody has beaten it in nine years.”
“Don’t.”
“I’m not consoling you, I’m telling you the finding.”
“He’s a fucking slogan, Renny.”

“Yes.” He didn’t flinch from it. “And in about four years, roughly eleven million people are going to say it to each other at parties, and not one of them will know it belonged to a man, and they will all be describing the same thing he described, and every single one of them will be right.” He picked the foam back up. “That’s what happens to true things. They get sold. It doesn’t stop them being true. It just stops them being yours.”
I asked him one more question that night. The last one I ever asked him.
“When it launches. When it’s fifteen minutes and a subscription and there’s an advert with a woman on a sofa. What happens to all this?”
Renny Shaw looked around a garage full of crates.

“It ends,” he said. “Immediately. Completely. Nobody will hold their breath for two minutes under a collapsing wave to reach a place they can reach on a Tuesday evening at home, and they shouldn’t, and I want you to hear me say that I think that’s good.” He taped a crate shut. “Four people died getting this. In four years nobody will ever have to die for it again. That’s the whole argument and it’s an extremely strong one and I’ve never found a way round it.”
“But.”
He looked up.

“But I’ve read four hundred and ninety-two reports,” he said, “and every one of them was written by somebody who paid for it. And I don’t know — I genuinely do not know, and I’ve thought about almost nothing else since Basel first called me — whether the thing they saw was the thing itself, or whether it was the price.”
He put his hand flat on the taped lid.

“You can synthesise the state,” Renny said. “I don’t believe for one second that you can synthesise the cost. And I have no idea, none, whether what those forty-one people found in the dark was a room, or whether it was just what four minutes of dying looks like to someone who has spent four years earning the right to be there.”
The rain went on.
“They’ll find out in Basel,” he said. “That’s their problem now. My part’s finished.”
PROTOCOL IV. NOTE TO THE FILE
Appended 04 February. Not for circulation. Retained with the corpus.
I am closing this document because the work is finished and because I would like there to be one honest page in the box.

Everything before this was written to be read by people who were going to go under. I have reread all of it this week and it is, in every technical respect, correct. The tables are correct. The rungs are correct. The physiology is correct and I would defend any line of it to any panel.
It is also a recruitment document, and I knew that when I wrote it, and I want that recorded in my own hand rather than inferred later by somebody kinder than me.

A man does not read four pages on the architecture of the door and then go back to his tables. He goes and finds a wave. That was the mechanism. I did not build it by accident; I have written training material for the Ministry of Defence and I know precisely how a document persuades. Protocol I gives you the science, which earns your trust. Protocol II gives you a ladder with a top you cannot see, which is the oldest trick in any liturgy. Protocol III tells you to surrender, and tells you that you will not want to come back, and tells you to come back anyway — for us.

Every man and woman who went down went of their own choice. I have never once lied to any of them and no one was ever coerced. Both of those statements are true and neither of them is a defence, and I have stopped pretending otherwise.
Corpus at close: forty-one subjects, four hundred and ninety-two runs, one hundred and fifty at Rung Four or deeper with telemetry. Delivered.

Four did not return. R. Moura, 26. B. Krall, 26. M. Sadr, 30. And a name I will not put in a file that is going to Basel, because his mother is still alive in Setúbal and has been told a different story, and that is the one thing in nine years I have chosen to keep out of the ledger.
Against those four: a compound in preclinical development which will, if it clears, deliver the same state to anyone who wants it in fifteen minutes with no water, no cold, no fear and no risk.
That is a good trade. I have run it every way and it remains a good trade and I want whoever reads this to understand that I am not tortured about the arithmetic.
What I am unsure about is smaller and will not fit on a slide.

I have four hundred and ninety-two reports and every one of them was written by somebody who paid for it. I do not know whether what they found was the thing itself or the receipt. I do not know whether a man who has spent four years learning to be still while he is being killed sees a room because a room is there, or because four years of that is what a room costs.
They will find out in Basel, at scale, cheaply, on sofas.

I would give a great deal to be told the answer and I will not be, because I am fifty-eight and my chest went in 1997 and the one thing I have never been able to buy, from anyone, at any price, is a single one of the four hundred and ninety-two.
A final instruction, which supersedes the rest.

To any subject reading this: the ladder is closed. There is nothing further from me. Go home. Take the tables with you if you like, they are good for you and they are the only part of this that will make you healthier.
Do not go looking for the join. It is going to be for sale.
— R.S.
TWENTY-TWO. THE COUNT

Renny Shaw went to Basel on the eleventh of February and I have not seen him since. He sent one message in April, three words long — It cleared phase one — and I did not reply, and there has been nothing after that.
The pool in the old town went back to being a pool. Somebody finally painted over the dolphin.

Kirill Novak got a new sponsor and moved to Chile, which is what Mina said he’d do, in the first conversation I ever had with her, sitting on the second chair in a flat that smelled of neoprene. He’s alive as of last month. I check occasionally, which I’m not proud of.

Iker Aramendi stopped. Completely. Nineteen years old, walked away in February, went back to Zarautz and works for his uncle doing something with refrigeration units. He sent me a photograph of a van at Christmas. No message with it. Just a van.
Léo has not ridden and will not ride.

The energy drink company with the lightning bolt going into a fist ran a campaign in the summer built around a slow-motion wipeout with a piano on it. Not Beto’s. They used somebody else’s. Beto’s is still up, in its original form, with the comments open, and it has done sixteen million now.
And in about three years — four, maybe, these things take longer than the deck says — there is going to be an advertisement.

I’ve thought about it more than is healthy. I’ve built the whole thing in my head. A woman in her thirties on a sofa in a room with good light. Fifteen minutes. No supervision required. Some warm, quiet voice at the end reading the six words my brother said lying on his back on wet sand with the ocean running out of his sinuses and a Sky Italia cameraman rewinding.
There’s a room down there.
And eleven million people will say it to each other, and they’ll be right, and not one of them will know it belonged to anybody.
I still drive.
That surprises people. I’ve had two writers and one documentary crew come to this town and every one of them wanted the version where I burned the ski, and I understand the appeal, and it isn’t true.

I’m out there most days there’s swell. I do the season. I’ve got a new impellor and eleven hundred and forty hours on the clock and the best hands on this coast, and there are nineteen-year-olds coming through now who’ve never heard of any of it, who think Beto Krall is a clip, who talk about content the way we used to talk about waves.
They go down and I go and get them.

And I get there in sixty-two seconds, because that is what I do, and because I have decided — deliberately, in full possession of everything in this book — that sixty-two seconds is the correct number and I am not going to move it.

Renny was right about the arithmetic and he was right about the corpus and he was right about my brother’s lungs and he was right about me being an instrument. He was wrong about exactly one thing, and it’s this: he thought I was the ceiling.
I’m not the ceiling.
I’m the floor.

Every man in that water gets to go as far as he goes because there is somebody in the channel counting, and the counting is the only thing on that entire coast that has never once been for sale, and I have four hundred and eighty-two of them now, and every single one came back.
The last thing.

There’s a morning in March when it’s twenty feet and clean and nobody’s out because the contest window has closed and everyone’s gone home to Hawaii and Biarritz and wherever. The cliff is empty. The lighthouse doesn’t sell tickets in March.
I take the ski out on my own on those mornings and I sit in the channel with the engine off.
It’s about six metres deep where I sit. Green water. No foam. On a calm day you can see the sand.

And I think about it every single time. Every time. I have thought about it on that spot maybe six mornings now — that I am forty-two years old and in reasonable condition and I have done fourteen months of tables in a flat above a garage where nobody can see me, and that I could take off the kill cord and go over the side and be at the bottom in eight seconds, and that nobody would be counting, because I am the only person in Europe who counts and I would be down there.
Seventy-nine seconds is what I’ve had. Once, in December, by accident.

I know exactly what’s on the other side of the alarm. I’ve been warm. I’ve had the quiet. I have seen the edges up and to the left and I have felt the interest come on, that calm unhurried curiosity, and I know with total certainty that if I go over the side on one of those March mornings I will get further than I got before, because I’m trained now, and because there’d be nobody arriving at sixty-two seconds to interrupt me.
I sit there with my hand on the kill cord.

And what stops me isn’t Ruy, and it isn’t Mina, and it isn’t fear, and it isn’t the fact that in four years I could buy it in a fifteen-minute dose for the price of a phone contract and drive an hour later.
It’s that somebody would have to come and get me.

Somebody would have to come out in a boat, on a flat morning in March, and find a forty-two-year-old man face down in six metres of clear water off an empty beach, and put their hand in his collar, and count, and be wrong about it for the rest of their life.
I’ve done that. I did it when I was thirty-two and I have not put it down since and I would not give it to anybody.

So I sit in the channel with the engine off, on the fifteenth of March, over six metres of green water with the sand visible at the bottom of it and nothing between me and the thing I want except a decision that has to be made again every single time.
And I start the engine.
And I go in.
GLOSSARY
Apam Napat [uh-PAAM nuh-PAAT] — Avestan, child of the waters.
An old Persian figure who lives at the bottom of the sea and holds the glory that men go down for.
Baleia [buh-LAY-uh] — Portuguese, whale. The bar in the old town, where Renny Shaw drinks tea in the back room with the notebook shut under his hand.
Khvarenah [khwuh-RE-nuh] — Avestan, glory. A light belonging to kings and to the world, which runs from the man who reaches for it and goes down into the water; the book’s third part is named for it.
O teimoso [oo tay-MOH-zoo] — Portuguese, the stubborn one.
What the narrator’s mother called his brother, said the way a doctor says a diagnosis.

Samba [SAM-buh] — Portuguese, a Brazilian dance. The fine fast tremor that runs through the shoulders and jaw of a diver coming up from a brain that has been running low on oxygen, named after the dance because there was nothing else to call it.
It means the lights are flickering; no samba, in an unconscious man, means they are off.
